en: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad

The dawn, indeed, is the head of the sacrificial horse; the sun is its eye, the wind its breath, and Vaiśvānara fire its open mouth. The year is the body of the sacrificial horse. The sky is its back, the atmosphere its belly, the earth its underbelly, the quarters its flanks, the intermediate quarters its ribs, and the seasons its limbs. The months and half-months are its joints; days and nights are its feet; the stars are its bones; the clouds are its flesh; the undigested food in the stomach is the sand; the rivers are its intestines; the liver and the lungs are the mountains; and the herbs and trees are its hair. Its forepart is the rising sun, and its hindpart is the setting sun. When it yawns, that is lightning; when it shakes itself, that is thunder; when it urinates, that is rain. Speech, indeed, is its voice. 1.1.1.

Day indeed was born as the Mahiman cup before the horse; its womb is in the eastern ocean. Night was born as the Mahiman cup behind it; its womb is in the western ocean. These two Mahiman cups were produced on both sides of the horse. Having become a *haya*, it carried the gods; as a *vājī*, the Gandharvas; as an *arvan*, the Asuras; and as a *aśva*, human beings. The ocean alone is its kin, the ocean its womb. 1.1.2.
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa.

In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here. This world was covered by death, which is hunger; for hunger is indeed death. He created the mind, thinking, "May I have a self. He moved about performing *arcana* (worship/striving). As he performed *arcana*, water was produced. "Surely, while I was performing *arcana*, *ka* (pleasure/water) has come into being," he thought. That is the reason for the name *arka*. Indeed, pleasure (*ka*) comes to him who knows this reason for the name *arka*. 1.2.1.

The waters, indeed, are the *arka*. That which was the froth of the waters solidified; it became this earth. Upon it he exerted himself. From him, thus exerted and heated, his essence as vital energy (*tejas*) emerged: fire. 1.2.2.

He divided himself threefold: the sun as one third and Vāyu as one third. This very breath is thus divided threefold. Of it, the eastern direction is the head, and those two [intermediate directions] are the two arms. Then, the western direction is its tail, and those two [intermediate directions] are the two thighs. The south and the north are the two sides; the sky is the back, the intermediate space is the belly, and this earth is the chest. This breath is established in the waters; wherever it goes, it is established there by one who knows thus. 1.2.3.

He desired: "Let a second self be born from me. Through his mind, he entered into union with speech—[speech being] hunger, which is death. That which was the seed became the year; for prior to that, there was no year. He bore him for as long as a year is; at the end of that time, he brought him forth. When he was born, he opened his mouth to devour him. The child cried out "Bhāṇ! That became speech. || 1.2.4 ||

He thought, "If I should think of this [world] as food, I shall make it less. With that speech and with that self, he created all this—whatever there is: the *ṛg* verses, the *yajus* formulas, the *sāman* chants, the meters, the sacrifices, progeny, and cattle. Whatever he created, he resolved to eat. He eats everything; that is the essence of Aditi’s name, "Aditi" (the Eater). Whoever knows this essence of Aditi’s name, "Aditi," becomes the eater of all this, and everything becomes his food. 1.2.5.

He desired, "May I sacrifice again with a greater sacrifice. He exerted himself; he practiced austerity. From him, thus exerted and heated by austerity, glory and vigor departed. Glory and vigor are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). When the vital breaths had departed, his body began to swell. His mind remained fixed upon that very body. 1.2.6.

He desired: "May this [world] be fit for sacrifice (*medhya*) for me; may I be possessed of it through my self. From that, the horse (*aśva*) came into being. Because it became fit for sacrifice (*aśvat*), that is precisely why the Horse Sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is called *aśvamedha*. He who knows it thus, truly knows the Horse Sacrifice. He thought of it as something not yet fully enclosed. At the end of a year, he sacrificed it for himself; he offered the other animals to the deities. Therefore, they sacrifice the sprinkled horse, which belongs to all the deities, as belonging to Prajāpati. This indeed is the Horse Sacrifice: he who shines yonder (the sun). A year is his self. This fire here is the *arka* (flame). These worlds are its selves. These two, the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*, become again a single deity: Death itself. He conquers recurrent death; death does not reach him. Death becomes his self. He becomes one with these deities. 1.2.7.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa.

There were two classes of Prajāpati’s offspring: the gods and the asuras. Of these, the gods were the younger and the asuras were the elder. They contended for these worlds. Then the gods said, "Come, let us overcome the asuras at the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha. 1.3.1.

They said to Speech, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," Speech sang the Udgītha for them. Whatever enjoyment was in Speech, that she sang for the gods; whatever is auspicious that she speaks, that she sang for herself. They perceived, "Verily, they will overcome us by means of this singer. Having rushed upon him, they pierced him with evil. That which is evil, namely whatever one speaks that is improper—that indeed is that evil. 1.3.2.

Then they said to the breath, "Sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [said] Prāṇa; he sang the Udgītha for them. Whatever enjoyment was in Prāṇa, that he sang for the gods; whatever is pleasant that he smells, that [he kept] for himself. They understood: "Verily, with this singer, they will surpass us. Rushing toward him, they pierced him with evil. That which is this unpleasant thing one smells—that indeed is that evil. 1.3.3.

Then they said to the eye, "Sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [said the eye], and the eye sang the Udgītha for them. Whatever enjoyment was in the eye, that it sang for the gods; whatever was beautiful that it saw, that it sang for itself. They knew, "With this singer, they will surely surpass us. Rushing toward it, they pierced it with evil. That which is evil is precisely that which one sees here as unseemly; that indeed is that evil. 1.3.4.

Then they said to the ear, "Chant the Udgītha for us. "So be it," it replied, and the ear chanted for them. Whatever enjoyment there is in the ear, that it secured for the gods; whatever is pleasant that it hears, that it secured for itself. They perceived, "With this chanter, they will surely surpass us. They rushed upon it and pierced it with evil. That evil is precisely what one hears here that is improper; that indeed is that evil. 1.3.5.

Then they said to the mind, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [said] the mind; it sang the Udgītha for them. Whatever enjoyment was in the mind, that it sang for the gods; whatever is a good intention, that it sang for itself. They perceived, "Surely, by this singer they will surpass us. Having rushed upon it, they pierced it with evil. That which is evil is precisely that which one here intends improperly; that indeed is that evil. In this very way, they beset these deities with evils; in this very way, they pierced them with evil. 1.3.6.

Then they said to this breath in the mouth, "Do thou sing the udgītha for us. "So be it," said that breath, and it sang the udgītha for them. They perceived, "Verily, by means of this singer, they will overcome us. They rushed at him and sought to pierce him with evil. Just as a clod of earth would crumble upon hitting a stone, even so did they crumble away and perish in all directions. Thereupon the gods prospered and the asuras were defeated. He who knows this prospers in himself, and his hateful rival is defeated. 1.3.7.

They said, "Where indeed has he been who has thus attached himself to us? "He was here within the mouth," they replied. He is *Ayāsya Āṅgirasa*, for he is the essence (*rasa*) of the limbs (*aṅga*). This deity is named *Dūṛ* (the Far). For death is far from her. And death becomes far from him who knows this. This deity, having struck away evil and death from these deities, caused them to go to where these quarters end. There she deposited their evils. Therefore, one should not approach people, nor should one approach the edge of a place, thinking, "Lest I fall into evil and death."

This very deity, having struck away the evil of death from these deities, then carried them beyond death. First, it carried speech beyond [death]. When speech was released from death, it became fire; that fire, having transcended death, shines beyond it. Then it carried the breath beyond [death]. When the breath was released from death, it became wind; that wind, having transcended death, blows beyond it. Then it carried the eye beyond [death]. When the eye was released from death, it became the sun; that sun, having transcended death, burns beyond it. Then it carried the ear beyond [death]. When the ear was released from death, it became the quarters; those quarters have transcended death beyond it. Then it carried the mind beyond [death]. When the mind was released from death, it became the moon; that moon, having transcended death, shines beyond it. Indeed, this deity carries beyond death him who knows thus.

Then he sang for himself the song for the sake of food. For whatever food is eaten is eaten by him alone; thus he finds firm support here. The gods said, "This entire world is indeed as much as food. You have sung that for yourself. Grant us a share in this food! He replied, "In that case, enter into me. They said, "So be it," and they entered into him on all sides. Therefore, when one eats food with this [breath], these [other breaths] are satisfied by it. Verily, his own people enter into him who knows this: he becomes the supporter of his own, the best, the leader, the eater of food, and the sovereign. But whoever among his own seeks to oppose one who knows this does not have the power over those dependent on him. On the other hand, whoever follows him, or whoever among his dependents seeks to follow him, he indeed has the power over those dependent on him.

Thus, this is the Aṅgirasa of the limbs, for he is the essence (rasa) of the limbs. Breath (prāṇa), indeed, is the essence of the limbs; for breath is truly the essence of the limbs. Therefore, from whichever limb the breath departs, that very limb withers. For this, indeed, is the essence of the limbs. 1.3.19.

He indeed is Bṛhaspati. Speech is the *bṛhatī*; he is her lord, therefore he is Bṛhaspati. (1.3.20) He indeed is Brahmaṇaspati. Speech is the *brahman*; he is her lord, therefore he is Brahmaṇaspati. (1.3.21) He indeed is the Sāman. Speech is the Sāman; it is both "she" (*sā*) and "he" (*ama*), and that constitutes the essence of the Sāman. Furthermore, because he is equal to a white ant, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, and equal to this entire universe—for that reason also he is the Sāman. He who knows this Sāman attains union with and residence in the same world as the Sāman. (1.3.22) He indeed is the Udgītha. Breath is "ut," for by breath all this is upheld. Speech is the "gīthā. It is both "ut" and "gīthā," and thus it is the Udgītha. (1.3.23)

Moreover, Brahmadatta Caikitāneya, while consuming the King [Soma], said: "May this King strike off the head of that man who sang the High Chant for him other than Ayāsya Āṅgirasa! For he indeed sang the High Chant with speech and with breath. 1.3.24.

Now, he who knows the property of this very Sāman comes into possession of property. Its property, indeed, is its tone (*svara*). Therefore, one intending to perform the priestly office (*ārtvijya*) should desire tone in his voice; with that voice endowed with tone, he should perform the priestly office. For this reason, people at a sacrifice desire to see one who possesses tone, as well as one who has property. He who thus knows the property of the Sāman comes into possession of property. (1.3.25)
He who knows the gold of this very Sāman—verily, gold comes to him. Its gold, indeed, is its tone (svara). Gold comes to him who thus knows the gold of this Sāman. 1.3.26.
He who knows the support of this Sāman becomes firmly established. Speech, indeed, is its support; for it is in speech that this breath is established when it is sung. "In food," some say. 1.3.27.
Now, therefore, follows the ascending of the *pavamāna* chants. The *prastotṛ* indeed begins the *sāman*. When he is about to begin it, he should mutter these [formulas]:
"Lead me from non-existence to existence; lead me from darkness to light."
"From death, lead me to immortality."

When he says, "Lead me from non-existence to existence," non-existence is indeed death and existence is immortality; thus he says, "Lead me from death to immortality; make me immortal. When he says, "Lead me from darkness to light," darkness is indeed death and light is immortality; thus he says, "Lead me from death to immortality; make me immortal. When he says, "Lead me from death to immortality," there is nothing here that is obscure. Now, regarding the other hymns (*stotra*s), he should sing for himself the attainment of food. Therefore, in those [other hymns], he may choose whatever boon he desires. This Udgātṛ who knows this sings for himself or for the sacrificer whatever desire he may wish for. And this is truly world-conquering. There is no hope for the lack of a world for one who thus knows this Sāman. 1.3.28n.
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa.

In the beginning, this universe was only the Self (ātman) in the form of a person (puruṣavidha). Looking around, he saw nothing other than himself. He first uttered, "I am. From that, the name "I" arose. Therefore, even today, when addressed, one first says, "It is I," and then pronounces whatever other name one may have. Because he burned away (auṣat) all evils before all this [universe], he is called Puruṣa. Verily, he who knows this burns away anyone who seeks to surpass him. 1.4.1.

He was afraid. Therefore, one who is alone is afraid. He then reflected: "Since there is nothing other than myself, of what am I afraid? Thereupon his fear vanished. For of what could he have been afraid? Indeed, fear arises from a second [entity]. || 1.4.2 ||

He truly did not find delight. Therefore, one who is alone does not find delight. He desired a second. He became as large as a man and a woman in close embrace. He caused this very Self to fall into two parts. From that, there arose the husband and the wife. Therefore, Yājñavalkya used to say: "This body is, as it were, only half of oneself. Therefore, this void is filled by a woman. He united with her, and from that, human beings were born. 1.4.3.

He then reflected: "How indeed can I procreate after having produced myself alone? Well, let me become invisible. She became a cow, and the other became a bull; he united with her, and from that cows were born. The one became a mare and the other a stallion; the one became a she-ass and the other a donkey; he united with them, and from that the solid-hoofed animals were born. The one became a she-goat and the other a goat; the one became a ewe and the other a ram; he united with them, and from that goats and sheep were born. In this very manner, whatever pair there is, even down to the ants, all that he created. 1.4.4.
He knew: "I am indeed the creation, for I have created all this. From that, he became the creation. Whoever knows this comes to exist within this creation of his. 1.4.5.

Then he churned. From his mouth and from his hands he created fire. Therefore, these two are hairless on the inside; for the womb is hairless on the inside. Thus, when they say, "Sacrifice to that one, sacrifice to that one," regarding each individual deity, it is merely the manifestation of this very [Brahman]. For he alone is all the gods. Now, whatever here is moist, that he created from semen; that is Soma. All this world is indeed just this much: food and the eater of food. Soma is the food, and Agni is the eater of food. This is the "excessive creation" (*atisṛṣṭi*) of Brahman: that he created the gods, who are superior, while he himself was mortal; and that being mortal, he created those who are immortal. Therefore it is called the "excessive creation. He who knows this prospers through this excessive creation of his. 1.4.6.

At that time, this world was indeed undifferentiated. It was differentiated by name and form alone—as "this one has such a name" and "this one has such a form. Even now, this world is differentiated by name and form alone—as "this one has such a name" and "this one has such a form. This very Self has entered here even to the tips of the fingernails, like a razor placed in a razor-case, or like fire in its source. People do not see it, for it is incomplete [when perceived through specific functions]. When breathing, it is called breath; when speaking, speech; when seeing, sight; when hearing, hearing; when thinking, mind. These are merely names derived from its activities. Whoever worships any one of these individually does not know, for it is incomplete through any one of them alone. One should worship it simply as the "Self," for in this all these become one. This is the track to be followed of this whole world, for by means of this Self one knows all this. Just as one finds [lost cattle] by following a footprint, so he who knows this finds fame and praise. 1.4.7.

This very Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else—this Self which is more internal. If someone were to say to one who speaks of anything other than the Self as dear, "He will lose what is dear to him," he would likely be right. One should worship the Self alone as dear. For one who worships the Self alone as dear, his dear ones do not perish.

Regarding this they say: "What indeed was that Brahman which, knowing it, men think, 'Through the knowledge of Brahman we shall become everything'? What was that Brahman by which all this came to be? (1.4.9)

In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman. It knew only itself: "I am Brahman. Therefore, it became all this. Whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he alone became that; so it was with the seers, and so with human beings. Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva attained [this realization]: "I became Manu, and I became the Sun. Even today, whoever knows this—"I am Brahman"—he becomes all this. Neither the gods nor anyone else can prevent his success, for he becomes their very self. But he who worships another deity, thinking, "He is one and I am another," does not know. He is like an animal to the gods. Just as many animals serve a man, even so each individual person serves the gods. When even a single animal is taken away, it is unpleasant; how much more so when many are? Therefore, that is not pleasing to them—that men should know this. 1.4.10.

In the beginning, this universe was indeed Brahman, one alone. Being alone, it did not flourish. It emitted from itself that superior form, the Kṣatra—the ruling powers among the gods, namely Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna. Therefore, there is nothing higher than the Kṣatra. For this reason, in the Rājasūya sacrifice, the Brāhmaṇa sits below the Kṣatriya; he thus bestows glory upon the Kṣatra. This Brahman is the source of the Kṣatra. Therefore, even if a king attains the highest position, in the end he resorts to Brahman as his own source. But he who harms him goes to his own source [in ruin]; he becomes worse, just as one who has harmed a superior. 1.4.11.
He did not multiply. He created the Viś. Those which are these classes of gods that are enumerated by their groups—the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśve Devas, and the Maruts. 1.4.12.
He did not multiply. He created the Śūdra caste, Pūṣan. This earth is indeed Pūṣan, for she nourishes everything here, whatever exists. 1.4.13.

He did not flourish at all. He emitted from that excellent form Dharma. This Dharma is the ruler of the ruling power (kṣatra); therefore, there is nothing higher than Dharma. Thus, even one who is weaker hopes against one who is stronger by means of Dharma, just as [one hopes] by means of a king. That which is Dharma is indeed Truth. Therefore, they say of one speaking the truth, "He speaks Dharma," and of one speaking Dharma, "He speaks the truth. For these two are indeed one and the same. 1.4.14

This [Brahman] is the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra. Among the gods, it became the Brahman through Agni; among humans, it became the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya through the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya through the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra through the Śūdra. Therefore, among the gods, people desire their world in Agni alone; among humans, they desire it in the Brāhmaṇa, for it was through these two forms that the Brahman came into being. Now, whoever departs from this world without having seen his own world, it does not support him, being unknown to him—just as a Veda that has not been studied, or any other work that has not been performed. Even if one who knows not thus performs a great meritorious deed, it surely perishes in the end for him. One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world. He who meditates upon the Self alone as the world—his work is never exhausted; for from this very Self, whatever he desires, that he creates. (1.4.15)

Moreover, this self (*ātman*) is indeed the world (*loka*) of all beings. When he offers oblations and performs sacrifices, by that he becomes the world of the gods. When he recites the sacred verses (*anubrūte*), by that he becomes the world of the seers (*ṛṣis*). When he makes offerings to the ancestors and desires offspring, by that he becomes the world of the ancestors. When he provides lodging for men and gives them food, by that he becomes the world of men. When he finds grass and water for the animals, by that he becomes the world of the animals. And when dogs, birds, and even creatures down to the ants subsist on what is in his house, by that he becomes their world. Just as one would desire safety for one’s own world, so do all beings desire safety for one who knows this. This, indeed, has been known and deliberated upon. 1.4.16.

In the beginning, this universe was the Self alone, just one. He desired: "May I have a wife, so that I may procreate; may I have wealth, so that I may perform ritual action. This much indeed is desire. Even if one seeks, one finds nothing beyond this. Therefore, even today, a solitary person desires: "May I have a wife, so that I may procreate; may I have wealth, so that I may perform ritual action. As long as he does not obtain even one of these, he considers himself incomplete. Now, his completeness is as follows: the mind is his self; speech is his wife; the vital breath is his offspring; sight is human wealth—for by sight one acquires it; hearing is divine wealth—for by hearing one hears it; the self itself is his ritual action—for by means of the self one performs action. This sacrifice is fivefold; the animal is fivefold; man is fivefold; all this that exists here is fivefold. Whoever knows this obtains all this. (1.4.17)
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa.
When the Father, through wisdom and austerity, produced the seven kinds of food,
he made one common to all, and two he assigned to the gods.
He made [one] for himself; he gave one to the cattle. Upon that everything is established—both that which breathes and that which does not.
Why do they not perish, even though they are being consumed all the time? He who indeed knows that imperishability eats food with his very face.
He goes unto the gods; he lives upon vital strength.
Thus end the verses. 1.5.1.

“That the Father produced seven kinds of food by means of wisdom (*medhā*) and austerity (*tapas*)”—for indeed, the Father produced them by means of wisdom and austerity. “One of these is common to all”—this very food which is eaten here is that one which is common to all. He who venerates this does not turn away from evil, for this is mixed. “Two he assigned to the gods”—the *huta* (the offering into the fire) and the *prahuta* (the offering elsewhere). Therefore, they offer and present offerings to the gods; and thus they say, “The New and Full Moon sacrifices. Therefore, one should not be a frequent performer of the *iṣṭi* sacrifices. “One he gave to the cattle”—that is milk. For it is milk indeed that humans and cattle live upon in the beginning. Therefore, when a child is born, they first feed him either clarified butter or make him suckle at the breast. And they say of a newborn calf, “It has not yet grazed on grass. Upon that [milk] everything is established—both that which breathes and that which does not. For upon milk everything is established—both that which breathes and that which does not. Now, regarding what they say: “By offering milk for a year, one conquers repeated death”—one should not understand it in that way. On the very day one offers [milk], on that very day one who knows thus conquers repeated death, for he gives all food to the gods. Why do those [foods] not perish, even though they are being eaten constantly? Man is indeed the imperishable (*akṣiti*). For he produces this food again and again. “He who knows that imperishable”—man is indeed the imperishable. For he produces this food through every act of thought and through his works. If he were not to do this, it would indeed perish. “He eats food with his face”—the face is the *pratīka*; that is to say, with his mouth. “He goes to the gods, he lives upon strength”—this is a praise. 1.5.2.

"He made three for himself"—namely, mind (*manas*), speech (*vāk*), and breath (*prāṇa*). These he made for himself. "I was elsewhere in mind, I did not see; I was elsewhere in mind, I did not hear"—for it is by the mind alone that one sees, and by the mind that one hears. Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are nothing but the mind. Therefore, even when touched from behind, one perceives it through the mind. Whatever sound there is, that is speech alone; for it is dependent on the end (the mouth), and it does not go beyond it. Out-breath (*prāṇa*), in-breath (*apāna*), diffused breath (*vyāna*), upward breath (*udāna*), and equalizing breath (*samāna*)—all these are nothing but breath. This self (*ātman*) consists of this: it consists of speech, it consists of mind, and it consists of breath. 1.5.3.
These three worlds are these very [three]: speech is this world, mind is the intermediate world, and breath is that world. 1.5.4.
The three Vedas are these very [three]: speech is the Ṛgveda, the mind is the Yajurveda, and the breath is the Sāmaveda. 1.5.5.
The gods, the ancestors, and humans are these very things: speech indeed is the gods, mind is the ancestors, and breath is humans. 1.5.6.
The father, the mother, and the offspring indeed exist. Mind alone is the father, speech is the mother, and breath is the offspring. 1.5.7.

The known, the object of desire to know, and the unknown—these alone [are all things]. Whatever is known is a form of speech; for speech is the knower. Having become that, speech protects him. Whatever is the object of desire to know is a form of the mind; for the mind is the object of desire to know. Having become that, the mind protects him. Whatever is unknown is a form of the vital breath; for the vital breath is the unknown. Having become that, the vital breath protects him. 1.5.8–10.
Of that speech, the earth is the body; its form of light is this fire. Therefore, as great as speech is, so great is the earth, and so great is this fire. 1.5.11.

Now, heaven is the body of this mind; its form of light is yonder sun. As great as the mind is, so great is heaven; as great as yonder sun is, so great is that [mind]. These two united in sexual intercourse; from that, breath was born. That is Indra. He is without a rival. For a rival is indeed a second person. He who knows this has no rival. 1.5.12.

Now, water is the body of this vital breath (*prāṇa*); its form of light is that moon over there. As great as the vital breath is, so great are the waters; as great as the waters are, so great is that moon. All these are indeed equal, all are infinite. Verily, he who meditates upon these as finite wins a finite world; but he who meditates upon these as infinite wins an infinite world. 1.5.13.

This very year, Prajāpati, consists of sixteen parts (*kalā*). Of him, the nights are fifteen parts; his sixteenth part is the constant (*dhruvā*) one. By means of the nights, he waxes and wanes. On the night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), having entered into all these living beings by means of this sixteenth part, he is born again from there in the morning. Therefore, on that night, one should not deprive any living being of its life—even a chameleon—for the sake of honoring this very deity. 1.5.14.

That Prajāpati, the year consisting of sixteen parts, is indeed this very person who knows thus. His wealth constitutes fifteen parts; his own self is the sixteenth part. By means of his wealth, he is filled up and by means of it he is diminished. That which is this self is the nave, and wealth is the felly. Therefore, even if one suffers the loss of everything, as long as one lives by means of the self, people say, "He has lost only the felly. || 1.5.15 ||

Now, there are indeed three worlds: the world of men, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods. This world of men is to be won by a son alone, and not by any other ritual act; the world of the fathers by ritual acts; and the world of the gods by knowledge. Of all the worlds, the world of the gods is indeed the best; therefore, they praise knowledge. 1.5.16.

Now, therefore, follows the transmission. When he thinks he is about to depart this world, he says to his son: "Thou art the Brahman; thou art the sacrifice; thou art the world. The son replies: "I am the Brahman; I am the sacrifice; I am the world. For whatever has been studied, all that is unified in the term "Brahman"; whatever sacrifices there are, all those are unified in the term "sacrifice"; and whatever worlds there are, all those are unified in the term "world. This whole world is indeed just this much. [Thinking: "May this [son], being all this, protect me from here," they say of a son who has been thus instructed that he is "world-winning. Therefore, they instruct him. When one who knows this departs from this world, he enters his son together with these very vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Whatever has been done by him improperly, from all that the son delivers him; therefore he is called "son" (*putra*). Through the son alone he finds firm support in this world. Then these divine, immortal vital breaths enter into him. 1.5.17

From the earth and from Agni, divine speech enters him. That indeed is divine speech by which whatever one speaks comes to be exactly so. From the sky and from Āditya, divine mind enters him. That indeed is divine mind by which one becomes only blissful and does not grieve. From the waters and from the moon, divine breath enters him. That indeed is divine breath which, whether moving or not moving, is not distressed and does not suffer injury. He who knows this becomes the self of all beings. As is this deity, so is he; and as all beings protect this deity, so do all beings protect him who knows this. Whatever these creatures grieve over, that belongs only to them; only merit goes to him. Indeed, evil never reaches the gods.

Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into the vows (*vratamīmāṃsā*). Prajāpati created the vital functions (*karmāṇi*). Once created, they vied with one another. Speech took up the resolve: "I shall speak"; the eye: "I shall see"; the ear: "I shall hear. And so did the other functions according to their respective roles. Death, becoming weariness (*śrama*), overtook them; he reached them, and having reached them, Death held them captive. Therefore, speech indeed becomes weary; the eye becomes weary; the ear becomes weary. But he did not reach this one, who is the central breath (*madhyamaḥ prāṇaḥ*). They resolved to find out about him: "He is indeed the best among us, for whether moving or not moving, he neither suffers nor is harmed. Come, let us all assume his very form! They all assumed his form. Therefore, these are called by the name "breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*). By that name, indeed, one speaks of the family in which a person is born who knows this. And whoever vies with one who knows thus withers away; having withered away, he finally dies. This is with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). 1.5.21.

Now, with respect to the deities: "I shall indeed blaze," so thought Agni; "I shall give heat," so thought Āditya (the Sun); "I shall shine," so thought Candramas (the Moon). In this manner, other deities [thought] according to their respective domains. Just as the middle vital breath among these vital breaths, so is Vāyu among these deities. For the other deities set, but not Vāyu. This deity, which is Vāyu, is the one that never sets. 1.5.22.
Now there is this verse:
"From whence the sun rises and wherein it sets. Verily, from the vital breath (prāṇa) it rises, and into the vital breath it sets.
The gods made that their law, saying: "That indeed is so today, and that shall be so tomorrow."

Or rather, whatever these [ancients] undertook then, they do that very same thing even today. Therefore, one should observe only a single vow: one should breathe out and breathe in, thinking, "Lest evil death should overcome me. If, however, one should undertake it, he should desire to complete it; by that, he wins union with and residence in the same world as this deity. 1.5.23.
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa.

This [universe] is indeed a triad: name, form, and action. Of these names, speech is their *uktha*; for from it all names arise. This is their *sāman*; for this is equal to all names. This is their *brahman*; for this supports all names. 1.6.1.
Now, among forms, the eye is their *uktha*, for from it all forms arise. It is their *sāman*, for it is equal to all forms. It is their *brahman*, for it sustains all forms. 1.6.2.

Now, "the self" is the *uktha* of these ritual acts, for from it all ritual acts arise. It is their *sāman*, for it is equal to all ritual acts. It is their *brahman*, for it sustains all ritual acts. These three, being real, are this one self; and this one self, being real, is these three. This is the immortal covered by the real. Breath (*prāṇa*) indeed is the immortal; name and form are the real; by these two this breath is covered. 1.6.3.
Thus ends the sixth Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the first chapter.

There was once a proud Gārgya Bālāki, a man well-versed in the Vedas. He said to Ajātaśatru, the king of Kāśī, "I shall tell you about Brahman. Ajātaśatru replied, "We give a thousand [cows] for such a speech! People indeed run about crying, 'Janaka! Janaka! (2.1.1)

Gārgya said: "The person who is there in the sun—that is the one I venerate as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I venerate him rather as the one who stands over all beings, the head, the king. He who venerates him thus becomes one who stands over all beings, the head, the king. 2.1.2.

Gārgya said: "The person who is yonder in the moon—that is the one I venerate as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I venerate him rather as the Great One, clad in white, King Soma. He who venerates him thus has [Soma] pressed and poured out for him day after day; his food does not fail. 2.1.3.

Gārgya said: "The person who is there in lightning—that is the one I venerate as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I venerate him rather as 'the radiant. He who venerates him thus becomes radiant, and his offspring become radiant. 2.1.4.

Gārgya said: "The person who is right here in space—that is the one I venerate as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I venerate him rather as the 'Full' that does not move away. He who venerates him thus is filled with offspring and cattle; his lineage does not perish from this world. 2.1.5.

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the wind—that very one I meditate upon as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as Indra Vaikuṇṭha, the unconquered army. He who meditates upon him thus becomes victorious, unconquerable, and a vanquisher of enemies. || 2.1.6 ||

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the fire—that is the one I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru replied: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the overcomer. He who worships him thus becomes an overcomer, and his offspring become overcomers. || 2.1.7 ||

Gārgya said: "This very person who is here in the waters—that is the one I venerate as Brahman. Ajātaśatru replied: "Do not talk to me about him! I venerate him rather as 'The Counterpart' (Pratirūpa). He who venerates him as such, a counterpart indeed approaches him, and not a non-counterpart; moreover, a counterpart is born from him. || 2.1.8 ||

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the mirror—him indeed I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the Radiant' (rociṣṇu). He who worships him thus becomes radiant; his offspring becomes radiant; and moreover, whatever he encounters, he outshines them all. 2.1.9.

Gārgya said: "This very sound that rises up behind a person as they walk away—that is what I venerate as Brahman. Ajātaśatru replied: "Do not talk to me about him! I venerate him rather as 'Life' (asuḥ). He who venerates him as such attains a full lifespan in this world; his vital breath does not leave him before the appointed time. || 2.1.10 ||

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the quarters—him indeed I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the second' and 'the inseparable. He who worships him thus becomes possessed of a companion; his retinue is never severed from him. || 2.1.11 ||

Gārgya said: "This very person who consists of shadow—that is the one I venerate as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I venerate him rather as Death. He who venerates him in this way attains a full lifespan in this world; death does not come to him before his time. || 2.1.12 ||

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the self—that very one I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the possessed of self' (ātmanvī). He who worships him thus becomes possessed of self; his offspring become possessed of self. Gārgya then became silent. 2.1.13.

Ajātaśatru said: "Is it merely that much? Gārgya replied: "It is merely that much. Ajātaśatru said: "By this much alone, [Brahman] is not known. Gārgya said: "Let me come to you as a pupil. || 2.1.14 ||

Ajātaśatru said: "It would indeed be contrary to the natural order for a Brāhmaṇa to approach a Kṣatriya with the thought, 'He will teach me the Brahman. Yet, I shall certainly make it known to you. Taking him by the hand, he rose up. They came upon a man who was asleep. He addressed him by these names: "Bṛhan! Pāṇḍaravāsa! Soma! Rājan! But he did not rise. He woke him by pressing him with his hand; then he rose. 2.1.15.
Ajātaśatru said: "When this person, who consists of consciousness, was thus asleep, where had he then been, and from whence did he now come? Gārgya did not know that. 2.1.16.

Ajātaśatru said: "When this person was asleep—this person who consists of consciousness—he takes to himself the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of his own consciousness and lies in that space which is within the heart. When he seizes them, then it is said of this person, 'He sleeps. Then the breath is indeed seized; speech is seized; the eye is seized; the ear is seized; the mind is seized. "When he moves about in the state of dreaming, those are his worlds. Then he becomes, as it were, a great king; or he becomes, as it were, a great Brahmin; or he goes to various high and low places. Just as a great king, having taken his subjects with him, might move about as he pleases in his own kingdom, even so this one, having taken the vital breaths with him, moves about as he pleases in his own body. (2.1.17–18)

Now, when one is fast asleep and knows nothing of anything, there are seventy-two thousand channels called *hitā* that extend from the heart to the pericardium; having slipped down through them, he rests in the pericardium. Just as a young boy, or a great king, or a great Brahmin might sleep after reaching the height of bliss, even so does he rest then. 2.1.19.

Just as a spider moves along by means of its thread, or as tiny sparks fly out from a fire, even so from this Self all vital breaths, all worlds, all gods, and all beings emerge. Its secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "the Truth of truth. The vital breaths are indeed truth, and He is the truth of them. 2.1.20.
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa.

Verily, he who knows the infant together with its support, its counter-support, its pillar, and its tether, holds back seven hateful rivals. This very breath that is in the middle is indeed the infant; this [lower body] is its support, this [upper body] is its counter-support, the breath is the pillar, and food is the tether. 2.2.1.

Seven imperishable powers attend upon it. Those red streaks that are in the eyes—with them Rudra is connected to it; those waters that are in the eyes—with them Parjanya is connected; with the pupil, the Āditya; with what is black, Agni; with what is white, Indra. With the lower eyelash the earth is connected, and with the upper, the sky. The food of one who knows this does not perish. 2.2.2.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"A ladle with its opening below and its bottom above—
in it is placed glory of every form."
Of that non-existent one, there were seven seers on the shore; speech was the eighth, coming together with the sacred word (brahman).

"A ladle with its mouth turned downward and its bottom turned upward"—this refers to this very head, for this head is indeed a ladle with its mouth downward and its bottom upward. "In it glory, multiform, is deposited"—the vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the glory that is multiform; he thus speaks of the vital breaths. "Of it, the seven seers sit upon the bank"—the vital breaths are indeed the seers; he thus speaks of the vital breaths. "Speech as the eighth, attaining harmony with the Brahman"—for speech as the eighth attains harmony with the Brahman. 2.2.3.

These two are indeed Gotama and Bharadvāja; this one is Gotama, this one is Bharadvāja. These two are indeed Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni; this one is Viśvāmitra, this one is Jamadagni. These two are indeed Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa; this one is Vasiṣṭha, this one is Kaśyapa. Speech itself is Atri, for by speech food is eaten. "Atri" is indeed a name for "eater. He who knows this becomes the eater of all; everything becomes his food. 2.2.4.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa.
There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless, the mortal and the immortal, the stationary and that which moves, and the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat). 2.3.1.

That which is other than air and the intermediate space is this formed [world]; it is mortal; it is stationary; it is the existent (*sat*). Of this formed world, of this mortal, of this stationary, of this existent, the essence is that which shines yonder. For this is the essence of the existent. (2.3.2)

Now, that which is formless consists of wind and the intermediate space. This is immortal; this is moving; this is the "Tyam. Of this formless, of this immortal, of this moving, of this "Tyam," the essence is this person who is in that orb, for he is indeed the essence of the "Tyam. Thus far with respect to the divine. 2.3.3.

Now, with respect to the self: that which is other than the vital breath and this space within the self is indeed the formed. This is mortal; this is stationary; this is being. Of this formed, of this mortal, of this stationary, of this being, this is the essence: namely, the eye. For this is the essence of being. 2.3.4.

Now, that which is formless consists of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and this space within the self. This is the immortal; this is the *yat*; this is the *tyat*. Of this formless, of this immortal, of this *yat*, of this *tyat*, the essence is this person who is in the right eye. For he is indeed the essence of the *tyat*. 2.3.5.

The form of this very person is like a garment dyed with safflower, like white wool, like a firefly, like the flame of a fire, like a lotus, like a sudden flash of lightning. Indeed, the splendor of one who knows this becomes like a sudden flash of lightning. Now, therefore, follows the instruction: "Not this, not this. For there is nothing else higher than this "not this. Now, its name is "the Truth of truth. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the truth; he is the truth of them. 2.3.6.
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa.
"Maitreyī," Yājñavalkya said, "I am indeed about to depart from this state. Come, let me make a final settlement between you and Kātyāyanī. 2.4.1.

Maitreyī said: "If, O Venerable Sir, this entire earth filled with wealth were mine, would I become immortal through that? "No," said Yājñavalkya, "your life would be just like the life of those who possess means; there is no hope for immortality through wealth. || 2.4.2 ||
Maitreyī said: "What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal? Tell me only that which you know, O Blessed One. (2.4.3)
Yājñavalkya said: "Truly, you are dear to us, and being so, you speak what is dear. Come, sit down; I shall explain it to you. But as I explain, you must meditate upon it. 2.4.4.

He said: "Truly, it is not out of love for the husband that the husband is dear, but it is out of love for the Self (*ātman*) that the husband is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the wife that the wife is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the wife is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the sons that the sons are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the sons are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for wealth that wealth is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that wealth is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the Brahminhood (*brahman*) that the Brahminhood is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the Brahminhood is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the Kshatriyahood (*kshatra*) that the Kshatriyahood is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the Kshatriyahood is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the worlds that the worlds are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the worlds are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the gods that the gods are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the gods are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for beings (*bhūta*) that beings are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that beings are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for everything that everything is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that everything is dear. Verily, the Self, O Maitreyī, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. By the seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing of the Self, all this is known. (2.4.5)

Brahman deserts him who knows Brahman as other than the Self; the Kṣatra deserts him who knows the Kṣatra as other than the Self; the worlds desert him who knows the worlds as other than the Self; the gods desert him who knows the gods as other than the Self; beings desert him who knows beings as other than the Self; everything deserts him who knows everything as other than the Self. This is Brahman, this is the Kṣatra, these are the worlds, these are the gods, these are beings, this is everything—that which is this Self. 2.4.6.

"Just as, when a drum is being beaten, one cannot grasp its external sounds, but by grasping the drum or the beating of the drum, the sound is grasped; (2.4.7) just as, when a conch is being blown, one cannot grasp its external sounds, but by grasping the conch or the blowing of the conch, the sound is grasped; (2.4.8) just as, when a lute is being played, one cannot grasp its external sounds, but by grasping the lute or the playing of the lute, the sound is grasped; (2.4.9) just as, from a fire kindled with damp fuel, various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, my dear, these—the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvāṅgirasa, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, sciences, Upaniṣads, verses, aphorisms, explanations, and commentaries—are the breath of this great Being. These indeed are its exhalations. (2.4.10) Just as the ocean is the one point of convergence for all waters, so the skin is the one point of convergence for all touches; so the two nostrils are the one point of convergence for all smells; so the tongue is the one point of convergence for all tastes; so the eye is the one point of convergence for all forms; so the ear is the one point of convergence for all sounds; so the mind is the one point of convergence for all thoughts; so the heart is the one point of convergence for all branches of knowledge; so the two hands are the one point of convergence for all actions; so the organ of generation is the one point of convergence for all pleasures; so the anus is the one point of convergence for all excretions; so the feet are the one point of convergence for all paths; so speech is the one point of convergence for all Vedas. (2.4.11) Just as a lump of salt thrown into water would dissolve right into the water, and it would not be possible to take it out again, yet wherever one might taste the water, it would be salty—just so, my dear, this great Being is infinite, boundless, and a mass of pure consciousness. Arising from these elements, it vanishes back into them. After death, there is no consciousness, I say, my dear. Thus spoke Yājñavalkya. (2.4.12)

Maitreyī said: "Right here, my lord, you have bewildered me by saying that there is no consciousness after death. He replied: "Indeed, I do not speak a bewildering thing. This is sufficient for understanding. For where there is duality, as it were, there one smells another; there one sees another; there one hears another; there one speaks to another; there one thinks of another; there one perceives another. But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he smell? Then by what and whom should he see? Then by what and whom should he hear? Then by what and to whom should he speak? Then by what and of whom should he think? Then by what and whom should he perceive? By what, my dear, should one perceive him by whom all this is perceived? By what, my dear, should one perceive the perceiver? (2.4.14)
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa.

This earth is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this earth. And that radiant, immortal person who is in this earth, and that radiant, immortal person who is in the body with respect to the self (*adhyātma*)—he is indeed this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 2.5.1 These waters are honey for all beings; all beings are honey for these waters. And that radiant, immortal person who is in these waters, and that radiant, immortal person who is in the semen with respect to the self—he is indeed this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 2.5.2 This fire is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this fire. And that radiant, immortal person who is in this fire, and that radiant, immortal person who consists of speech with respect to the self—he is indeed this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 2.5.3 This wind is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this wind. And that radiant, immortal person who is in this wind, and that radiant, immortal person who is the breath (*prāṇa*) with respect to the self—he is indeed this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 2.5.4 This sun is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this sun. And that radiant, immortal person who is in this sun, and that radiant, immortal person who is the visual one with respect to the self—he is indeed this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 2.5.5 These quarters are honey for all beings; all beings are honey for these quarters. And that radiant, immortal person who is in these quarters, and that radiant, immortal person who is the auditory one, the echo, with respect to the self—he is indeed this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 2.5.6 This moon is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this moon. And that radiant, immortal person who is in this moon, and that radiant, immortal person who is the mental one with respect to the self—he is indeed this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 2.5.7 This lightning is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this lightning. And that radiant, immortal person who is in this lightning, and that radiant, immortal person who is the luminous one with respect to the self—he is indeed this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 2.5.8 This thunder is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this thunder. And that radiant, immortal person who is in this thunder, and that radiant, immortal person who is the sonorous one with respect to the self—he is indeed this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 2.5.9

This space is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this space. And that person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this space, and that person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is here in the self within the space of the heart—this indeed is that which is the Self, this is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. || 2.5.10 ||

This Dharma is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this Dharma. And that person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is in this Dharma, and that person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is the Dharma-self (dhārma) within the self—this indeed is that which is the Self, this is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 2.5.11.

This truth is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this truth. And that person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is in this truth, and that person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is in the self (adhyātma) as truth—he is indeed this very Self, this immortality, this Brahman, this All. 2.5.12.

This human being is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this human being. And that person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is here in this human being, and that person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is here with respect to the self (adhyātma) as the human being—he is indeed this Self; he is this immortality, he is this Brahman, he is this All. 2.5.13.

This Self is honey for all beings; all beings are honey for this Self. And that person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this Self, and this Self consisting of light and consisting of immortality—that is indeed this Self, this immortal, this Brahman, this All. 2.5.14.

This very Self is the overlord of all beings, the king of all beings. Just as all the spokes are fixed in the nave and the felloe of a chariot wheel, even so in this Self all beings, all gods, all worlds, all vital breaths, and all these selves are fixed. 2.5.15

This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the Aśvins. Seeing this, the seer declared: "O Heroes, I make manifest for you two that fierce deed for the sake of gain, even as thunder makes rain manifest—namely, how Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, with the head of a horse, spoke this honey to you."
This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the Aśvins. Seeing this, the seer declared:
"O Aśvins, for Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, you restored the horse's head;
he, observing the Truth, proclaimed the honey to you—the Tvaṣṭṛ-made [knowledge] which was hidden in your secret place, O wonder-workers."
This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the Aśvins. Seeing this, a seer declared:
"He made bodies with two feet; he made bodies with four feet.
Having first become a bird, he, the Puruṣa, entered into the bodies."
Verily, this person dwells within all cities; there is nothing whatsoever that is not enveloped by him, and there is nothing whatsoever that is not covered by him. 2.5.18.

This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the two Aśvins. Seeing this, a seer declared: "He has become the counterpart of every form; such is his form for the sake of being perceived. Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion (*māyā*), for ten hundred bay steeds are harnessed to him."

This indeed is the yellow-hued one; this indeed is the ten, the thousands, the many, and the infinite. This very Brahman is without beginning, without end, without interior, and without exterior. This Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all. Such is the instruction. 2.5.19.
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa.

Now, the lineage (*vaṃśa*). Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana; Gaupavana from Pautimāṣya; Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana; Gaupavana from Kauśika; Kauśika from Kauṇḍinya; Kauṇḍinya from Śāṇḍilya; Śāṇḍilya from both Kauśika and Gautama; [and] Gautama from Āgniveśya; Āgniveśya from both Śāṇḍilya and Anabhimlāta; Anabhimlāta from Anabhimlāta; Anabhimlāta from Anabhimlāta; Anabhimlāta from Gautama; Gautama from both Saitava and Prācīnayogya; Saitava and Prācīnayogya from Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from both Bhāradvāja and Gautama; Gautama from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Vaijavāpāyana; Vaijavāpāyana from Kauśikāyani; Kauśikāyani from Ghṛtakauśika; Ghṛtakauśika from Pāraśaryāyaṇa; Pāraśaryāyaṇa from Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Jātūkarṇya; Jātūkarṇya from both Āsurāyaṇa and Yāska; Āsurāyaṇa from Traivaṇi; Traivaṇi from Aupajandhani; Aupajandhani from Āsuri; Āsuri from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from Ātreya; Ātreya from Māṇṭi; Māṇṭi from Gautama; Gautama from Gautama; Gautama from Vātsya; Vātsya from Śāṇḍilya; Śāṇḍilya from Kaiśorya Kāpya; Kaiśorya Kāpya from Kumārahārita; Kumārahārita from Gālava; Gālava from Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya; Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya from Vatsanapāt Bābhrava; Vatsanapāt Bābhrava from Pathas Saubhara; Panthas Saubhara from Ayāsya Āṅgirasa; Ayāsya Āṅgirasa from Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra; Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra from Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra; Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra from the two Aśvins; the two Aśvins from Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa from Atharvan Daiva; Atharvan Daiva from Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana; Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana from Pradhvaṃsana; Pradhvaṃsana from Ekarṣi; Ekarṣi from Vipracitti; Vipracitti from Vyaṣṭi; Vyaṣṭi from Sanāru; Sanāru from Sanātana; Sanātana from Sanaga; Sanaga from Parameṣṭhin; Parameṣṭhin from Brahmā; Brahmā is self-existent (*svayaṃbhu*). Homage to Brahmā! 2.6.1–2.6.3
Thus ends the sixth Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the second chapter.

Janaka of Videha performed a sacrifice at which many gifts were bestowed. There, the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas had gathered together. Janaka of Videha desired to know: "Who among these Brahmins is the most learned in the Vedas? He enclosed a thousand cows; ten padas of gold were fastened to each pair of horns. He said to them: "Venerable Brahmins, let him who among you is the most learned in the Veda drive away these cows. Those Brahmins did not dare to do so. Then Yājñavalkya said to his own pupil: "My dear Sāmaśrava, drive these cows away. He drove them away. The Brahmins were incensed, saying: "How can he call himself the most learned in the Veda among us? Now, Aśvala was the Hotṛ priest of Janaka of Videha. He questioned Yājñavalkya: "Are you indeed, O Yājñavalkya, the most learned in the Veda among us? He replied: "We pay homage to the one who is the most learned in the Veda; we are merely desirous of cattle. Thereupon, the Hotṛ Aśvala resolved to question him further.

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is overtaken by death, since all is seized by death, by what means does the sacrificer free himself from the reach of death? "By the Hotṛ priest, by the fire, and by speech. Speech, indeed, is the Hotṛ of the sacrifice. Now, that which is this speech is this very fire; it is the Hotṛ. That is liberation; that is complete liberation. (3.1.3)

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is pervaded by day and night, and all is encompassed by day and night, by what means does the sacrificer transcend the pervasion of day and night? "By the officiating priest, the Adhvaryu; by the eye, which is the sun. For the Adhvaryu is indeed the eye of the sacrifice. Now, that which is this eye is yonder sun; he is the Adhvaryu. That is liberation; that is complete liberation. (3.1.4)

"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is pervaded by the bright and dark fortnights, and all is encompassed by the bright and dark fortnights, by what means does the sacrificer transcend the pervasion of the bright and dark fortnights? "By the Udgātṛ priest, through wisdom, [that is] through the vital breath (prāṇa). For the Udgātṛ of the sacrifice is indeed the vital breath. Now, that which is this vital breath is Vāyu; he is the Udgātṛ; that is liberation; that is complete liberation. || 3.1.5 ||

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "by what means does the sacrificer ascend to the heavenly world from this atmosphere which is, as it were, without support? "By the Brahman-priest, by the mind, and by the moon. "The mind, indeed, is the Brahman-priest of the sacrifice. "Now, that which is this mind is yonder moon; he is the Brahman, he is liberation, he is complete liberation. Thus far the deliverances. Now, the attainments. 3.1.6.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "with how many ṛg-verses will this Hotṛ priest perform today at this sacrifice? "With three," he replied.
"Which are those three?"

The invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), the offering verse (*yājyā*), and the recitation (*śasyā*) as the third—what does one win by means of these? Whatever here exists that is endowed with breath. (3.1.7)
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many oblations will this Adhvaryu offer today in this sacrifice? "Three," [he replied].
"Which are those three?"
"Those oblations which blaze up when offered, those which overflow when offered, and those which settle down when offered—what does one win by them?

"By those oblations which blaze up when offered, one wins the world of the gods; for the world of the gods, as it were, blazes forth. By those oblations which overflow when offered, one wins the world of the fathers; for the world of the fathers, as it were, overflows. By those oblations which settle down when offered, one wins the world of men; for the world of men, as it were, lies low. (3.1.8)
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "with how many deities does this Brahman protect the sacrifice from the south today? "With one," he replied. "Which is that one?"
"It is mind alone. Mind is indeed infinite, and the All-Gods are infinite. By means of that [mind], he conquers an infinite world. 3.1.9.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many *stotriya* hymns will this Udgātṛ chant today at this sacrifice? "Three," he replied.
"Which are those three?"
The *puronuvākyā*, the *yājyā*, and the *śasyā* as the third—
what are these with respect to the self (*adhyātma*)?
The *puronuvākyā* is indeed the *prāṇa*, the *yājyā* is the *apāna*, and the *śasyā* is the *vyāna*.
"What does he conquer by means of them?
"By the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), he conquers the world of earth; by the offering verse (*yājyā*), the world of the intermediate space; by the recitation (*śasyā*), the world of heaven.
Thereupon, Aśvala the Hotṛ fell silent. 3.1.10.

Then Ārtabhāga Jāratkārava questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many are the *grahas* (seizers) and how many are the *atigrahas* (over-seizers)? "There are eight *grahas* and eight *atigrahas*.
"Which are those eight *grahas* and eight *atigrahas*? || 3.2.1 ||
The out-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the grasper; it is seized by the out-breath as the over-grasper, for by means of the out-breath one smells odors. 3.2.2.
Speech, indeed, is the grasper; it is seized by the name as the over-grasper, for by speech one utters names. 3.2.3.
The tongue, indeed, is a grasper; it is seized by taste as the over-grasper, for by means of the tongue one perceives tastes. 3.2.4.
The eye, indeed, is a grasper; it is seized by form as the over-grasper, for one sees forms with the eye. 3.2.5.
The ear, indeed, is the grasper; it is seized by sound as the over-grasper, for by means of the ear one hears sounds. 3.2.6.
The mind, indeed, is the grasper; it is seized by desire as the over-grasper, for by means of the mind one desires desires. 3.2.7.
The two hands are indeed the grasper; they are seized by action as the over-grasper, for it is with the two hands that one performs action. 3.2.8.
The skin, indeed, is a grasper; it is seized by touch as the over-grasper, for by means of the skin one perceives touches. Thus, these are the eight graspers and the eight over-graspers. 3.2.9.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is food for death, who is that deity for whom death is food? "Fire, indeed, is death; it is the food of water. He conquers recurrent death. (3.2.10)

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, do his vital breaths (*prāṇa*) depart from him, or not? "No," Yājñavalkya replied, "they are simply absorbed right here. He swells up, he becomes bloated, and bloated, the dead man lies there.

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, what does not leave him? "The name," [he replied]. "The name is indeed infinite, and the Viśvedevas are infinite. By means of that, he wins an infinite world. 3.2.12.

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "when the speech of this dead person enters into fire, his breath into the wind, his eye into the sun, his mind into the moon, his hearing into the quarters, his body into the earth, his self (ātman) into space, the hairs of his body into herbs, the hairs of his head into trees, and his blood and semen are deposited in the waters—where then does this person come to be? "Come here, gentle Ārtabhāga; let us two alone consider this matter, for it is not fit to be discussed in public. The two went out and deliberated. What they spoke of was indeed action (karman); what they praised was indeed action. "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and evil through evil action. Thereupon, Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga ceased questioning.

Then Bhujyu Lāhyāyani questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "we were traveling among the Madras as wandering students. We came to the house of Patañcala Kāpya. He had a daughter possessed by a Gandharva. We asked him, 'Who are you? He replied, 'I am Sudhanvan Āṅgirasa. When we asked him about the ends of the worlds, we then asked him, 'Where did the Pārikṣitas go? [We asked: 'Where did the Pārikṣitas go? I ask you this, Yājñavalkya: where did the Pārikṣitas go? " || 3.3.1 ||

He said: "He indeed spoke thus: 'They went, indeed, to where those who sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice go. [The other asked: 'Where, pray, do those who sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice go? [He replied: 'This world extends for thirty-two days' journeys of a god's chariot. The earth surrounds it on all sides, twice as large. The ocean surrounds the earth on all sides, twice as large again. Now, as wide as the edge of a razor or the wing of a fly, so wide is the space between them; Indra, having become a bird, delivered them to Vāyu. Vāyu, having placed them within himself, caused them to go to that place where the performers of the horse-sacrifice abide. Thus, in effect, he praised Vāyu alone. Therefore, Vāyu is the individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*), and Vāyu is the collective manifestation (*samaṣṭi*). He who knows this conquers recurrent death. Thereupon, Bhujyu Lāhyāyani ceased questioning. 3.3.2.

Then Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self that is within all. "This is your Self that is within all. "Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all?"

He who breathes in with the in-breath (*apāna*)—he is your Self, dwelling within all. He who breathes out with the out-breath (*prāṇa*)—he is your Self, dwelling within all. He who breathes through with the inter-breath (*vyāna*)—he is your Self, dwelling within all. He who breathes up with the up-breath (*udāna*)—he is your Self, dwelling within all. This is your Self, dwelling within all. 3.4.1.

Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa said: "Just as one might point out, 'That is a cow,' or 'That is a horse,' so has this been pointed out. Please explain to me that Brahman which is manifest and not hidden, the Self that is within all. "Yājñavalkya, this is your Self that is within all. "Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all?"

"You would not see the seer of seeing; you would not hear the hearer of hearing; you would not think the thinker of thinking; you would not discern the discerner of discerning. This is your Self, the innermost of all. Everything other than this is afflicted. Thereupon, Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa became silent. 3.4.2.

Then Kahola Kauṣītakeya questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all. "This is your Self, which is within all. "Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all?"

He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow and delusion, old age and death—having known this very Self, the Brahmins, rising above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, lead the life of mendicants. For the desire for sons is indeed the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is the desire for worlds; these two are both simply desires. Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship, should seek to abide in childlike innocence. Having become disillusioned with both childlike innocence and scholarship, he becomes a sage (*muni*). Having become disillusioned with both non-sagehood and sagehood, he becomes a true Brahmin. By what means could he be such a one? He is exactly such as he is by that [means]. Everything other than this is afflicted. Thereupon, Kahola Kauṣītakeya ceased questioning. 3.5.1.

Then Gārgī Vācaknavī questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," she said, "since all this is woven to and fro upon the waters, upon what, then, are the waters woven to and fro? "Upon the wind, Gārgī. "Upon what, then, is the wind woven to and fro? "Upon the worlds of the intermediate space, Gārgī.
"Upon what, then, are the worlds of the intermediate space woven to and fro? "Upon the worlds of the Gandharvas, Gārgī."
"In what, then, are the worlds of the Gandharvas woven to and fro? "In the worlds of Aditi, Gārgī.
"In what, then, are the worlds of Aditi woven to and fro? "In the worlds of the Moon, Gārgī.
"In what, then, are the worlds of the Moon woven to and fro? "In the worlds of the Stars, Gārgī."

"In what, indeed, are the worlds of the stars woven back and forth? "In the worlds of the gods, Gārgī. "In what, indeed, are the worlds of the gods woven back and forth? "In the worlds of Indra, Gārgī. "In what, indeed, are the worlds of Indra woven back and forth? "In the worlds of Prajāpati, Gārgī."
"In what, indeed, are the worlds of Prajāpati woven to and fro? "In the worlds of Brahman, Gārgī. "In what, indeed, are the worlds of Brahman woven to and fro?

He said, "Gārgī, do not ask beyond this! Lest your head shatter apart. You are asking beyond the deity that should not be asked beyond. Gārgī, do not ask beyond! Thereupon Gārgī Vācaknavī ceased questioning. 3.6.1.

Then Uddālaka Āruṇi questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "we were staying among the Madras at the house of Patañcala Kāpya, studying the sacrifice. His wife was possessed by a Gandharva. We asked him, 'Who are you? He replied, 'I am Kabandha Ātharvaṇa. He then spoke to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists: 'Do you know, O Kāpya, that Sūtra in which this world, the other world, and all beings are strung together? Patañcala Kāpya replied, 'I do not know it, venerable sir. He then spoke to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists: 'Do you know, O Kāpya, that Inner Controller who controls from within this world, the other world, and all beings? Patañcala Kāpya replied, 'I do not know him, venerable sir. He then spoke to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists: 'O Kāpya, whoever knows that Sūtra and that Inner Controller—he is a knower of Brahman, he is a knower of the worlds, he is a knower of the gods, he is a knower of the Vedas, he is a knower of beings, he is a knower of the Self, he is a knower of all. Thus he spoke to them."
"I know that. If you, Yājñavalkya, being ignorant of that thread and that inner controller, drive away the cows of Brahman, your head shall fall off.
"I do indeed know that thread and that inner controller, O Gautama," he said.
"Whoever might say here, 'I know, I know,' tell us how you know it. (3.7.1)

He said: "Vāyu indeed, O Gautama, is that thread. By Vāyu as the thread, O Gautama, this world, the other world, and all beings are held together. Therefore, O Gautama, they say of a dead man: 'His limbs have fallen apart,' for by Vāyu as the thread, O Gautama, they are held together. "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya. Speak of the Inner Controller. 3.7.2

He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.3.

He who, dwelling in the waters, is within the waters, whom the waters do not know, whose body the waters are, who controls the waters from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.4.
He who, dwelling in fire, is within fire, whom fire does not know, whose body is fire, who controls fire from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.5.

He who, dwelling in the intermediate space, is within the intermediate space, whom the intermediate space does not know, whose body is the intermediate space, who controls the intermediate space from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. 3.7.6.
He who dwells in the wind, yet is within the wind, whom the wind does not know, whose body is the wind, who controls the wind from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.7.
He who dwells in heaven, yet is within heaven, whom heaven does not know, whose body is heaven, who controls heaven from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.8.
He who, dwelling in the sun, is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body the sun is, who controls the sun from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. 3.7.9.

He who, dwelling in the quarters, is internal to the quarters; whom the quarters do not know; whose body the quarters are; who controls the quarters from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. 3.7.10.

He who dwells in the moon and the stars, yet is within the moon and the stars, whom the moon and the stars do not know, whose body the moon and the stars are, who controls the moon and the stars from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who dwells in space, yet is within space, whom space does not know, whose body is space, who controls space from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.12
He who, dwelling in darkness, is within darkness, whom darkness does not know, whose body is darkness, who controls darkness from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.13
He who dwells in fire, yet is within fire, whom fire does not know, whose body is fire, who controls fire from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.14.

Now, with respect to the elemental (adhibhūta): He who dwells in all beings, yet is within all beings; whom all beings do not know, whose body all beings are, and who from within controls all beings—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. This is with respect to the elemental. 3.7.15.

Now, with respect to the self: He who dwells in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), yet is within the vital breath; whom the vital breath does not know; whose body is the vital breath; who controls the vital breath from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. 3.7.16.
He who, dwelling in speech, is within speech, whom speech does not know, whose body is speech, who controls speech from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.17
He who, dwelling in the eye, is within the eye, whom the eye does not know, whose body is the eye, who controls the eye from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.18
He who dwells in the ear, yet is within the ear, whom the ear does not know, whose body is the ear, who controls the ear from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.19
He who, dwelling in the mind, is within the mind, whom the mind does not know, whose body is the mind, who controls the mind from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.20.
He who, dwelling in the skin, is within the skin, whom the skin does not know, whose body is the skin, who controls the skin from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. 3.7.21.

He who dwells in consciousness, yet is within consciousness, whom consciousness does not know, whose body is consciousness, who controls consciousness from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 3.7.22.
"He who dwells in semen, yet is within semen, whom semen does not know, whose body is semen, who controls semen from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

Unseen, He is the Seer; unheard, He is the Hearer; unthought, He is the Thinker; unknown, He is the Knower. There is no other seer than He, there is no other hearer than He, there is no other thinker than He, there is no other knower than He. He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Everything else but Him is subject to suffering. Thereupon, Uddālaka Āruṇi ceased questioning. 3.7.23.
Thus ends the seventh Brāhmaṇa.

Then Vācaknavī said: "Venerable Brahmins, come, I shall ask him two questions. If he can explain them to me, then indeed none of you will ever defeat him in this debate concerning Brahman. "Ask, Gārgī," [Yājñavalkya replied]. (3.8.1)

She said: "O Yājñavalkya, just as a warrior from Kāśī or Videha, the son of a noble father, might rise up having strung his unstrung bow and taken two arrows in his hand that pierce through enemies, even so have I risen up against you with two questions. Answer them for me. "Ask, Gārgī," he said. (3.8.2)

She said: "Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two—the sky and the earth—and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—across what is that woven, warp and woof? (3.8.3)

He said: "O Gārgī, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—across all this, [the Brahman] is woven like warp and woof. (3.8.4)
She said: "Homage be to you, Yājñavalkya, who has explained this to me; hold it for another. "Ask, Gārgī," he replied. (3.8.5)
