She said: "Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—in what are all these woven to and fro? (3.8.6)

He said: "Gārgī, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—all that is woven, warp and woof, upon space alone. "But upon what, then, is space woven, warp and woof? (3.8.7)

He said: "Gārgī, this is indeed that syllable which the Brāhmaṇas declare to be neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily, neither shadowy nor dark, neither air nor space; it is without attachment, without taste, without smell, without eye, without ear, without speech, without mind, without radiance, without breath, without mouth, and without measure; it has nothing inside and nothing outside. Nothing whatsoever eats it, and no one whatsoever eats it. (3.8.8)

"Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart. Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart. Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the moments, the hours, the days and nights, the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the years stand held apart. Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, some rivers flow eastward from the white mountains, and others flow westward, or toward whatever direction they may be. Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, humans praise one who gives, the gods [favor] the sacrificer, and the ancestors depend upon the ladle."

"Or, Gārgī, whoever in this world offers oblations, sacrifices, or performs austerities for many thousands of years without knowing this Imperishable—one's [merit] becomes merely finite. Or, Gārgī, whoever departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is pitiable. But he, Gārgī, who departs from this world having known this Imperishable, is a true Brāhmaṇa. (3.8.10)

Now, this very syllable, O Gārgī, is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower. There is no other seer than this; there is no other hearer than this; there is no other thinker than this; there is no other knower than this. In this very syllable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof. 3.8.11.

She said: "Venerable Brahmins, you should consider yourselves fortunate enough if you can escape from me merely by paying homage. Truly, no one shall ever defeat you in this debate on Brahman. Thereupon, Gārgī Vācaknavī ceased questioning. 3.8.12.
Thus ends the eighth Brāhmaṇa.

Then Vidagdha Śākalya questioned him: "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? He answered with this very *nivid*: as many as are mentioned in the *nivid* of the Vaiśvadeva [hymn]: "Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three. "Yes," he said. "But how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Thirty-three. "Yes," he said. "But how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Six."

"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "Three," he replied. "Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "Two," he replied. "Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "One and a half," he replied.
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "One," he replied. "Om," he said. "Which are those three and three hundred, and three and three thousand? (3.9.1)
He said: "These are merely their manifestations; there are, in truth, only thirty-three gods.
"Which are those thirty-three?
"The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the twelve Ādityas—that makes thirty-one—and Indra and Prajāpati are the thirty-second and thirty-third."
"Who are the Vasus?
"Fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, the sun, the sky, the moon, and the stars—these are the Vasus. For in these all this wealth (vasu) is placed; therefore they are called the Vasus. 3.9.3.
"What are the Rudras?

"These ten vital breaths in a person, with the self as the eleventh. When they depart from this mortal body, they cause one to weep (√rud). Because they cause one to weep, they are called Rudras. (3.9.4)

"What are the Ādityas? "The twelve months of the year are these Ādityas; for they go along taking up everything here. Because they go along taking up everything here, therefore they are called Ādityas. 3.9.5.
"What is Indra? What is Prajāpati? "Indra is indeed the thunder, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice.
"What is the thunder?"
"The thunderbolt," he said.
"What is the sacrifice? "The sacrificial animals," he replied. 3.9.6.
Which are the six? Fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, the sun, and the sky—these are the six. For these indeed are all this as "the six. 3.9.7.
"Who are those three gods? "These very three worlds; for within these are all these gods.
"Who are those two gods? "Food and breath alone."
"What is the 'one-and-a-half'?
[It is] "this one which blows. Regarding this, they say: "Since this [wind] blows as if it were only one, how then is it 'one-and-a-half'?"
Because all this was contained within him, he is called "Adhyardha" (the One-and-a-Half). "Who is that one god?
"Prāṇa," he replied. "He is Brahman; they call him 'Tyat' (That). 3.9.9.

“He who knows that person whose abode is the earth itself, whose world is fire, whose light is the mind, and who is the ultimate resort of every self—he indeed would be a knower, Yājñavalkya. “I do know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak. It is this very person who is embodied. Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? “Immortality,” he replied. 3.9.10.
"He for whom desire is the abode, the heart the world, and the mind the light—verily, he who knows that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya.
"I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak. He is this very person consisting of desire. Name him, Śākalya; what is his deity? "Women," he replied.

"He for whom visible forms alone are the sphere, whose world is the eye, and whose light is the mind—he who would know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya. "I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak. That very person who is there in the sun, he is this one. "Speak on, Śākalya! Who is his deity? "Truth," he said. 3.9.12

“He for whom space alone is the abode, the ear the world, and the mind the light—verily, he who knows that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya. “I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak. That very person who is heard and who is heard back—that is he. “Speak on, Śākalya! What is his deity? “The quarters,” he said. 3.9.13.

"He whose abode is darkness, whose world is the heart, and whose light is the mind—he who knows that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya. "I do know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak. It is this very person consisting of shadow. Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "Death," he said. 3.9.14

"He for whom visible forms alone are the sphere, whose world is the eye, and whose light is the mind—he who knows that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya. "I do know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak. That very person who is here in the mirror is he. "Speak on, Śākalya! Who is his deity? "The vital breath (asuḥ)," he said.

"He for whom water is the abode, the heart the world, and the mind the light—whosoever should know that person as the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya. "I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak. That very person who is here in the waters—that is he. "Speak on, Śākalya! Who is his deity? "Varuṇa," he said. 3.9.16.

"He whose abode is semen, whose world is the heart, whose light is the mind—he who would know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya. "I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak. It is this very person consisting of the son. Speak on, Śākalya; what is his deity? "Prajāpati," he said. 3.9.17
"Śākalya," said Yājñavalkya, "have these Brahmins indeed made you their charcoal-burner?"

"Yājñavalkya," said Śākalya, "since you have outtalked the Brāhmaṇas of the Kurus and Pañcālas, what do you know as Brahman? "I know the quarters together with their deities and their foundations. "In that you know the quarters together with their deities and their foundations... (3.9.19)
"Which deity resides in this eastern direction? "The deity Aditya.
"In what is that Aditya established? "In the eye. "In what, then, is the eye established? "In forms (rūpa), for by means of the eye one sees forms."
"On what, then, are forms established? "On the heart," he said. "For by means of the heart one knows forms; for on the heart alone are forms established. "Just so, Yājñavalkya. 3.9.20.
"Which deity are you in this southern quarter? "Yama is my deity. "In what is that Yama established? "In the sacrifice.
"In what, then, is the sacrifice established? "In the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)."

"On what, then, is the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) established? "On faith (śraddhā)," he said. "For when one has faith, then one gives the sacrificial gift; for on faith alone is the sacrificial gift established. "On what, then, is faith established? "On the heart," he said. "For by the heart one knows faith; for on the heart alone does faith become established. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya. (3.9.21)
"Which deity resides in this western quarter? "Varuṇa is its deity.
"On what is Varuṇa established? "In the waters.
"On what, then, are the waters established? "In semen."

"On what, then, is semen supported? "On the heart. Therefore, they say of even a well-formed newborn child, "He has slipped as it were from the heart; he has been fashioned as it were from the heart," for on the heart alone is semen supported. "It is just so, Yājñavalkya. 3.9.22.

"Which deity resides in this northern direction? "The Moon is its deity. "On what is that Moon established? "On consecration (dīkṣā). "On what, then, is consecration established? "On truth. Therefore, they say to one who has been consecrated, "Speak the truth," for consecration is indeed established upon truth.
"On what, then, is truth established? "On the heart," he said. "For by means of the heart one knows truth; for on the heart alone is truth established. "Just so, Yājñavalkya. 3.9.23.
"Which deity resides in this fixed quarter? "Agni is its deity. "In what is that Agni established? "In speech.
"In what, then, is speech established? "In the heart."
"On what, then, is the heart established? (3.9.24)

"Ahallika! said Yājñavalkya. "If you were to think this [Brahman] exists elsewhere than in us, then dogs would surely eat it, or birds would tear it apart, were it to exist elsewhere than in us. (3.9.25)

"On what, then, are you and the self established? "On the out-breath (prāṇa). "On what, then, is the out-breath established? "On the in-breath (apāna). "On what, then, is the in-breath established? "On the inter-breath (vyāna)."
"On what, then, is the vyāna established? "On the udāna.
"On what, then, is the udāna established? "On the samāna."

This very Self is "not this, not this. It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; indestructible, for it is not destroyed; unattached, for it does not cling; unfettered, it does not suffer; it is not injured. These are the eight abodes, the eight worlds, the eight gods, and the eight persons. Having withdrawn and then retracted those persons, he passed beyond them—that person of the Upanishads I ask you about. If you do not explain him to me, your head shall shatter apart.
Śākalya did not know him; his head fell apart, and thieves even carried off his bones, thinking them to be something else.

Then he said, "Venerable Brahmins, let whoever among you desires it question me; or let all of you question me. Or, let me question whoever among you desires it; or let me question all of you. Those Brahmins did not dare to respond. 3.9.27.
He questioned them with these verses:
"As a tree is a great forest-plant, so is a person not otherwise;
his hairs are its leaves, and his outer skin is its bark."
From his skin alone flows the blood; from the skin comes the scab.
Therefore, when it is pierced, the sap flows out, just as from a tree that has been struck.
Its flesh is the shavings, its sinews are the inner bark, and its bones are the wood within; the marrow has been fashioned as a likeness of marrow.
When a tree is cut down, it grows back from its roots even more luxuriantly;
but when a mortal is cut down by death, from what root does he sprout forth again?
"Do not say 'from semen,' for that is born from the living;
like a tree growing from seed, rebirth after death occurs directly."
Just as a tree that they have uprooted with its very roots does not come into being again,
from what root does a mortal man, once cut down by death, sprout forth?
"Once born, he is not born again; who indeed could give birth to him?
Consciousness, bliss, Brahman—the gift and the supreme goal of the giver for one who stands firm knowing that."
Thus ends the ninth Brāhmaṇa.

Thus ends the third chapter. Janaka of Videha was seated [in his assembly hall]. Then Yājñavalkya arrived. Janaka said to him, "Yājñavalkya, for what purpose have you come? Do you seek cattle, or do you seek subtle [discussions]? He replied, "O Sovereign, it is for both. 4.1.1.
"Let us hear what someone has told you.
"Śailini told me: 'Speech, indeed, is Brahman.

Just as one who possesses a mother, a father, and a teacher would speak, so did Śailini say, 'Speech, indeed, is Brahman,' for what could there be for one who does not speak? [I said: "But did he tell you its abode and its support?"
"He did not tell me," [the king said].
"That is indeed one quarter, O Emperor," [Yājñavalkya replied].
"Do you, Yājñavalkya, tell us that for us."
Speech indeed is its abode, space its support; one should meditate upon it as intelligence.

"What is the nature of discernment (*prajñatā*), Yājñavalkya? "Speech alone, O Emperor," he said. "For by speech alone, O Emperor, a kinsman is recognized; the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ*, history, ancient lore, sciences, secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*), verses, aphorisms, expositions, commentaries, what is sacrificed, what is offered, what is given, what is drunk, this world and the next world, and all beings—by speech alone, O Emperor, these are recognized. Speech indeed, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman. Speech does not desert him, and all beings flow toward him, who, knowing this, venerates it as such, having become a god, he goes to the gods."
"I will give you a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.

Yājñavalkya replied, "My father thought that one should not accept a gift without having first instructed his pupil. "Whatever anyone has told you, let us hear that," [said Janaka]. "Udaṅka Śaulbāyana told me: 'Brahman is indeed breath (prāṇa).

Just as one who possesses a mother, a father, and a teacher would speak, so did Śaulbāyana say: 'Brahman is indeed breath. For what could there be for one who does not breathe? But he did not tell you its abode or its support."
"He did not tell me," [he said]. "He told you only a single quarter, O Emperor," [Yājñavalkya replied].
"Then do you, Yājñavalkya, tell it to us."

"Life-breath (*prāṇa*) is the abode, space (*ākāśa*) is the foundation; one should meditate upon this as 'the dear' (*priya*). "What is its dearness, Yājñavalkya? "It is life-breath itself, O Emperor," he said. "Indeed, O Emperor, for the sake of life-breath, one performs sacrifices for whom one should not sacrifice, and accepts gifts from those from whom one should not accept. Even there, there is the fear of death in whatever direction one goes—for the sake of life-breath itself, O Emperor. Life-breath, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman. Life-breath does not desert him; all beings flow toward him. Having become a god, he goes to the gods—this is for one who, knowing thus, meditates upon this."
"I will give you a thousand [cows] with a bull as the leader," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father thought that one should not accept a gift without having first instructed [the pupil]. "Whatever anyone has told you, let us hear that.
"Barku Vārṣṇa told me: 'The eye, indeed, is Brahman.'"

"Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might say, so did that Vārṣṇa say: 'The eye, indeed, is Brahman. For what would there be for one who does not see? But he did not tell you its abode and its support. "He did not tell me," [Janaka replied]. "That, O Emperor, is only one-footed."
"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya!
One should meditate upon this as having the eye as its abode, space as its foundation, and 'the True' (satya) as its essence.
What is the nature of 'the True,' Yājñavalkya?"

"It is the eye itself, O Emperor," he said. "For by means of the eye, O Emperor, when they say to one who sees, 'Have you seen?', he says, 'I have seen'; that becomes the truth. The eye, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman. The eye does not desert him; all beings flow toward him. Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, worships it.
"I shall give you a thousand [cows] with an elephant and a bull," said Janaka of Videha.

Yājñavalkya said: "My father thought that one should not take [gifts] without having instructed [his son]. Let us hear what someone told you. "What did he tell you? "Gārbhīvipīta Bhāradvāja told me: 'The ear, indeed, is Brahman.

Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher would speak, so did Bhāradvāja say: 'The ear, indeed, is Brahman,' for what could there be for one who does not hear? "But did he tell you its abode and its support?"
"He did not tell me," [the king said]. "He told you only a single quarter, O Emperor," Yājñavalkya replied. "Then do you, Yājñavalkya, tell us that."
"The ear indeed is the abode; space is its foundation. One should meditate upon it as 'the infinite' (ananta).

What is its infinity, Yājñavalkya? "The quarters themselves, O Emperor," he said. "Therefore, O Emperor, whichever quarter one may go to, one never reaches its end, for the quarters are indeed infinite. The quarters, O Emperor, are the ear. The ear, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman. The ear does not desert him; all beings flow toward him who, knowing this, meditates upon it as such. Having become a god, he goes to the gods."
"I shall give you a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father thought that one should not accept a gift without having first given instruction. "Then let us hear what someone else told you," [said Janaka].
"Satyakāma Jābāla told me: 'The mind, indeed, is Brahman.'"

"Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might say, so did Jābāla say: 'The mind, indeed, is Brahman. [When asked] 'What would there be for one without a mind? he replied, 'He told you its abode and its support.
[Śākalya said: 'He did not tell me that. [Jābāla replied: "O Emperor, this [Brahman] is indeed one-footed."

"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "The mind (*manas*) indeed is its abode, space (*ākāśa*) its foundation; one should worship it as bliss (*ānanda*). "What constitutes its blissfulness, Yājñavalkya? "The mind itself, O Emperor," he said. "For by means of the mind, O Emperor, one is drawn toward a woman; from her a son resembling him is born; that is bliss. The mind, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman. The mind does not desert him, and all beings flow toward him. Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, worships it thus."
"I shall give you a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father thought that one should not accept a gift without having first instructed his pupil. "Then let us hear what someone else told you," [Janaka said].
"Vidagdha Śākalya told me: 'The heart, indeed, is Brahman.'"

"Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might say, so did Śākalya say: 'The heart, indeed, is Brahman. [Yājñavalkya asked: 'For what would there be for one without a heart? [Śākalya] replied: 'He told you its abode and its support.
[Yājñavalkya said: 'He did not tell me that. [Yājñavalkya continued: 'This, O Emperor, is but one-footed.'"
"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya!
One should worship this as having the heart as its abode, space as its foundation, and stability as its support.
What, Yājñavalkya, is this stability?"

"It is the heart alone," he said, "O Emperor. The heart, O Emperor, is indeed the abode of all beings; the heart, O Emperor, is the foundation of all beings. For it is in the heart, O Emperor, that all beings are established. The heart, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman. The heart does not desert him; all beings flow toward him who, knowing this, worships it as such. Having become a god, he goes to the gods.
"I shall give you a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya said: "My father thought that one should not take [the teacher's fee] without having first instructed [the pupil]. || 4.1.7 ||
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa.

Janaka of Videha, descending from his seat of grass, said: "Homage to you, Yājñavalkya! Teach me. He replied: "O Emperor, just as one who is about to set out on a long journey would prepare a chariot or a boat, even so have you prepared yourself with these secret doctrines (upaniṣads). Now that you are thus adorned, wealthy, learned in the Vedas, and instructed in the secret doctrines—when you are released from this body, where will you go?
"I do not know that, O Venerable One, where I shall go," he said.
"Then, indeed, I shall tell you that, where you shall go," he replied.
"May the Blessed One speak," [he said]. 4.2.1.

This person who is in the right eye is indeed named Indha (the Kindler). Although he is Indha, they call him Indra by an indirect name, for the gods are fond of the indirect and dislike the direct. Now, this form of a person in the left eye is his wife, Virāj. The space within the heart is their place of union. Their food is that lump of blood which is within the heart. Their covering is that which is like a net within the heart. Their path for moving about is the channel that rises upward from the heart. Like a hair split a thousandfold, so are these channels called *hitā* established within the heart; through them, this [subtle essence] flows in and out. Therefore, this [self] becomes even more refined in its food than this corporeal self.

The eastern direction is his eastern vital breaths; the southern direction is his southern vital breaths; the western direction is his western vital breaths; the northern direction is his northern vital breaths; the upward direction is his upward vital breaths; the downward direction is his downward vital breaths; all directions are all his vital breaths.

"This very Self is defined as 'not this, not this. It is ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped; indestructible, for it is not destroyed; unattached, for it does not cling; unfettered, it neither trembles nor suffers harm. 'Truly, Janaka, you have attained fearlessness,' said Yājñavalkya. Janaka, the King of Videha, replied: 'May fearlessness come to you, O Yājñavalkya, you who have made known to us, O Blessed One, that which is fearless. Salutations to you! Here are the people of Videha, and here am I. 4.2.4.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa.

Yājñavalkya went to Janaka of Videha. He thought, "I will not speak. Now, when Janaka of Videha and Yājñavalkya were once engaged in conversation regarding the Agnihotra sacrifice, Yājñavalkya granted him a boon. He chose the right to ask any question he desired. Yājñavalkya granted it to him. Then the Emperor himself asked the first question. 4.3.1.

"Yājñavalkya, what is the light of this person? "The light of the sun, O Emperor," he said. "By the light of the sun alone, this person sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns. "Just so, Yājñavalkya. 4.3.2.

"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, what light does this person have? "The moon, indeed, becomes his light. "By the light of the moon alone he sits, moves about, performs actions, and returns. "It is exactly so, Yājñavalkya. (4.3.3)

"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, what light does this person have? "Fire indeed becomes his light. "With fire as his light, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns. "It is just so, Yājñavalkya. 4.3.4

"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, when the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, what light does this person have? "Speech itself becomes his light," [he replied]. "With speech as his light, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns. "Therefore, O Emperor, even in a place where one's own hand is not discerned, wherever speech issues forth, there he moves about by that very light. "It is just so, Yājñavalkya. (4.3.5)

"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, when the moon has set, when the fire has gone out, and speech has become silent, what light does this person have? "The self alone becomes his light," he replied. "By the light of the self alone, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns. (4.3.6)

"What is the self? It is this person consisting of consciousness, who is among the vital breaths, the light within the heart. Being the same [in both states], he wanders through both worlds; he meditates, as it were, and he moves about, as it were. For, having become a dream, he transcends this world and the forms of death. 4.3.7.
Indeed, this person, when being born and entering a body, becomes united with evils; when departing and dying, he leaves the evils behind. 4.3.8.

Now, this very person has two states: this world and the state of the other world. The intermediate state is the third, the state of dream. Abiding in that intermediate state, he beholds both states—this world and the state of the other world. Now, whatever course he takes toward the state of the other world, having entered upon that course, he beholds both evils and joys. When he falls asleep, taking a portion from this all-encompassing world, himself striking it out, himself fashioning it, he sleeps with his own radiance, with his own light. Here, this person becomes self-luminous. 4.3.9.

There are no chariots there, no draft animals, and no roads; yet he creates chariots, draft animals, and roads. There is no joy, no delight, and no rapture there; yet he creates joy, delight, and rapture. There are no ponds, lotus-pools, or rivers there; yet he creates ponds, lotus-pools, and rivers. For he is the creator. 4.3.10.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"Having struck down the bodily [self] by means of dream-sleep, the Unsleeping One looks down upon those who sleep;
taking the light, he returns again to his place—the golden Person, the solitary swan. (4.3.11)
Protecting his lower nest with his vital breath, having moved outside the nest as an immortal, he goes wherever he desires—an immortal, golden person, a solitary swan. 4.3.12.
Moving through high and low states within the realm of dreams, the god (the self) assumes many forms;
as if rejoicing with women, as if laughing, and even as if beholding terrors. 4.3.13.

"They see his garden, but no one sees him. "One should not wake him," they say; "for it would be difficult to treat him who does not return [to consciousness]. Moreover, they say: "This is indeed his place of waking; for whatever he sees while awake, he sees that even when asleep. In this state, this person becomes self-luminous. "I shall give a thousand [cows] to your honor. Speak further for the sake of liberation. 4.3.14.

Having indeed sported and roamed about in that state of serene composure, and having seen both good and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule and according to his source, toward sleep itself. Whatever he sees there, he does not carry over with him; for this person is unattached. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya," [said Maitreyī]. "I give you a thousand [cows], O Blessed One. Speak further only for the sake of liberation. 4.3.15.

Having enjoyed himself and wandered about in that dream state, and having seen both good and evil, he hastens back again by the same path and through the same opening toward the waking state. Whatever he sees there, he does not carry with him; for this person is unattached. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya," [said Janaka]. "I give you a thousand [cows], O Blessed One. Speak further only for the sake of liberation. 4.3.16.

Having indeed sported and roamed about in this state during that dream-end, and having seen both merit and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule and according to his origin, toward the end of sleep itself. 4.3.17.
Just as a great fish swims back and forth between both banks, the near and the far, even so this person moves between these two states: the state of dream and the state of waking. 4.3.18.

Just as in this space a hawk or a falcon, having flown about and become weary, folds its wings and remains intent on resting, even so this person hastens toward that end where, being asleep, he desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever. Now, these channels of his called *hitā* (the "beneficent") exist with a fineness like a hair split a thousandfold; they are filled with white, blue, brown, green, and red [fluids]. Now, when it seems to him as if they are killing him, as if they are overpowering him, as if an elephant is chasing him, or as if he is falling into a pit—whatever fear he saw while awake, that he imagines there through ignorance (*avidyā*). But when he thinks, "I am like a god," or "I am like a king," or "I myself am all this"—that is his highest world.
This, indeed, is his form that transcends all desire, free from evil, and fearless.

Just as a man embraced by a beloved wife knows nothing without and nothing within, even so this person, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), knows nothing without and nothing within. This, indeed, is his form in which all desires are attained, which is the desire for the Self alone, which is free from desire, and beyond sorrow. 4.3.21.

In this state, the father is no longer a father and the mother is no longer a mother; the worlds are no longer worlds, the gods are no longer gods, and the Vedas are no longer Vedas. In this state, the thief is no longer a thief and the killer of an embryo is no longer a killer of an embryo; the outcaste is no longer an outcaste, the son of a degraded woman is no longer such, the ascetic is no longer an ascetic, and the hermit is no longer a hermit. He is untouched by merit and untouched by evil. For at that time, he becomes one who has crossed over all the sorrows of the heart. (4.3.22)

Indeed, that which he does not see—he, though seeing, does not see it. For there is no loss of the seer’s vision, because of its imperishability. But there is no second thing, other than him and separate from him, that he might see. 4.3.23

Indeed, when he does not smell, it is because, though smelling, he does not smell; for there is no loss of the smeller’s power of smelling, because of its imperishability. Yet there is no second thing, other than and distinct from him, which he might smell. 4.3.24.

That which indeed does not taste, it is truly that which, while tasting, does not taste. For there is no destruction of the taster’s capacity to taste, because of its imperishability. But there is no second thing existing apart from it, distinct from it, which it might taste. 4.3.25.

Indeed, when one does not speak there, it is as if one were speaking even while not speaking. For there is no loss of the speaker’s power of speech, because of its imperishability. Yet, there is no second thing existing there, distinct from him, which he might speak. 4.3.26.

Verily, that which he does not hear there, he does not hear even though he hears; for there is no loss of hearing for the hearer, because of its imperishability. But there is no second thing there, distinct from him, which he might hear. 4.3.27.

Verily, that which one does not think there, he indeed thinks it though he does not think it; for there is no loss of the thinker’s power of thinking, because of its imperishability. But there is no second thing existing there, distinct from him, which he might think. 4.3.28.

Indeed, that which one does not touch while touching it, for there is no destruction of the toucher’s power of touching because of its imperishability; yet there is no second thing existing apart from it, distinct from it, which one might touch. 4.3.29.

Indeed, that which he does not perceive, he perceives even while not perceiving it. For there is no loss of the perceiver’s power of perception, because of its imperishability. But there is no second thing, other than and distinct from him, which he might perceive. 4.3.30.

Or where there might be something else, there one might see another, one might smell another, one might taste another, one might speak of another, one might hear another, one might think of another, one might touch another, and one might cognize another.

"He becomes one with water, a seer without a second. This, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman. Thus did Yājñavalkya instruct him. "This is his supreme goal; this is his supreme attainment; this is his supreme world; this is his supreme bliss. On a mere fraction of this very bliss do other beings subsist. (4.3.32)

That which is the highest bliss of humans is for one who has attained success and prosperity among men, who is the lord of others, and who is most abundantly endowed with all human enjoyments. Now, a hundredfold the bliss of humans is a single measure of bliss for the ancestors who have won their worlds. Now, a hundredfold the bliss of the ancestors who have won their worlds is a single measure of bliss in the world of the Gandharvas. Now, a hundredfold the bliss in the world of the Gandharvas is a single measure of bliss for the gods by action (*karmadeva*), those who attain divinity through their deeds. Now, a hundredfold the bliss of the gods by action is a single measure of bliss for the gods by birth (*ājānadeva*), and also for one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), free from evil, and unassailed by desire. Now, a hundredfold the bliss of the gods by birth is a single measure of bliss in the world of Prajāpati, and also for one who is learned in the Vedas, free from evil, and unassailed by desire. Now, a hundredfold the bliss in the world of Prajāpati is a single measure of bliss in the world of Brahman, and also for one who is learned in the Vedas, free from evil, and unassailed by desire. This indeed is the supreme bliss; this is the world of Brahman, O Emperor—thus spoke Yājñavalkya.
"Therefore, I give a thousand [cows] to the Blessed One. Speak further only for the sake of liberation.
At this, Yājñavalkya became afraid, thinking: "The wise king has hemmed me in from all sides.

Having enjoyed himself and wandered about in that state of dream, and having seen both good and evil, he hastens back again, according to the rule and according to his source, toward the waking state itself. 4.3.34.

Just as a well-balanced cart might go along making a sound, even so this embodied self, mounted by the conscious self, goes forth making a sound, when it becomes one whose breath is drawn upward. 4.3.35.

When he reaches this state of attenuation—whether through old age or by illness—and undergoes this attenuation, then, just as a mango, a fig, or a pipal fruit is released from its stalk, even so this person, being completely liberated from these limbs, hastens back again according to his direction and according to his source, for the sake of vital breath alone. 4.3.36.

Just as when a king is approaching, fierce criminals, charioteers, and village headmen prepare food, drink, and lodgings, thinking, "He is coming! He is arriving!"—even so, all beings prepare for one who knows this, thinking, "Brahman is coming! Brahman is arriving! 4.3.37.

Just as when a king is about to set out on a journey, fierce executioners, judges, charioteers, and village headmen gather around him, even so at the time of death all the vital breaths gather around this self, at which point one becomes gasping for breath. 4.3.38.
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa.

When this self reaches weakness and falls, as it were, into a state of confusion, then these vital breaths (prāṇas) gather around it. Taking up these particles of light, it descends into the heart itself. When this person within the eye turns away, then one becomes unaware of forms. 4.4.1.

"They say he becomes unified and does not see; they say he becomes unified and does not smell; they say he becomes unified and does not taste; they say he becomes unified and does not speak; they say he becomes unified and does not hear; they say he becomes unified and does not think; they say he becomes unified and does not touch; they say he becomes unified and does not cognize. Then the tip of this heart shines forth. By that light, this self departs—either through the eye, or through the head, or through other parts of the body. As he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) follows after him; as the vital breath departs, all the vital functions follow after it. He becomes possessed of consciousness; indeed, he enters [the next state] with consciousness. Knowledge and action take hold of him, as does his prior experience (pūrvaprajñā). 4.4.2.

Just as a caterpillar, having reached the end of a blade of grass, takes hold of another support and draws itself together toward it, even so this Self, having cast off this body and caused ignorance to depart, takes hold of another support and draws itself together toward it. 4.4.3.

Just as a goldsmith, taking a portion of gold, fashions another form that is newer and more beautiful, even so this self, having cast off this body and dispelled ignorance, fashions another form that is newer and more beautiful—whether it be the form of a parent, or of a gandharva, or of a deity, or of Prajāpati, or of Brahman, or of other beings.

Now, this self is indeed Brahman—consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of earth, consisting of water, consisting of air, consisting of space, consisting of fire, consisting of what is not fire, consisting of desire, consisting of what is not desire, consisting of anger, consisting of what is not anger, consisting of righteousness, consisting of unrighteousness, and consisting of everything. Thus, it is "consisting of this" and "consisting of that. According as one acts, according as one conducts oneself, so does one become. By doing good, one becomes good; by doing evil, one becomes evil. One becomes holy through holy action and evil through evil action. Now, they say: "This person consists of desire alone. As is his desire, such is his resolve; as is his resolve, such is the deed he performs; and whatever deed he performs, that he attains. 4.4.5.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"Attached to that very thing, he goes along with his karma and the subtle body (*liṅga*) wherein his mind is fixed.
Having reached the end of that karma, whatever he does here [in this world]..."
From that world, he returns again to this world for the sake of action.

Thus indeed is he who desires. Now, as for him who does not desire—he who is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is attained, whose desire is the Self—his vital breaths do not depart. Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman. 4.4.6.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"When all desires that dwell in his heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal; he attains Brahman even here."
"Just as the slough of a snake might lie dead and cast away upon an anthill, even so does this body lie. But this bodiless, immortal life-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed Brahman, it is indeed light.
"I give you a thousand [cows], O Venerable One," said Janaka of Videha. 4.4.7.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The path is subtle, far-reaching, and ancient; it has been touched by me and discovered by me alone.
By that path, the wise who know Brahman go from here upward to the heavenly world, being liberated."
Of that path, they say it is white, or blue, tawny, green, and red. This is the path discovered by Brahmā; by it goes the knower of Brahman, the doer of good, and the radiant one.
Into blind darkness enter those who worship ignorance; into a darkness even greater than that, as it were, enter those who delight in knowledge. 4.4.10.
"Blissless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness;
to them go after death those people who are ignorant and lacking in wisdom. (4.4.11)
If a person were to know the Self, thinking "I am this," desiring what and for the sake of whose desire would he suffer along with the body? 4.4.12

He who has discovered and awakened to the Self that has entered this body, which is a dense thicket of doubt—he is the maker of all, for he is the creator of everything; his world is indeed the world itself. 4.4.13
Only here do we truly exist; thus we know this. If we did not know it, there would be a great destruction.
Those who know it become immortal, while others enter only into suffering. 4.4.14
When he perceives this Self directly as the divine Lord of all that has been and is to be, he no longer feels aversion toward anything. || 4.4.15 ||
Because the year revolves with its days, therefore the gods worship it as the light of lights, as life, and as immortality. (4.4.16)
In whom the five classes of beings and space itself are established—him alone I consider the Self; knowing him as the immortal Brahman, I am immortal. 4.4.17
Those who know the breath of the breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, and the mind of the mind—they have perceived the ancient, supreme Brahman. 4.4.18.
It is to be perceived by the mind alone; there is no diversity whatsoever here. He who perceives diversity here goes from death to death. (4.4.19)
This immeasurable and eternal reality is to be perceived as one alone.
Stainless and higher than space, the Self is unborn, great, and eternal. (4.4.20)
Having understood that very [Self], a wise Brahmin should practice wisdom;
he should not ponder over many words, for that is a weariness of speech. (4.4.21)

This indeed is that great unborn Self, who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths; he who rests within that space inside the heart. He is the controller of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all. He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action. He is the Lord of all, he is the ruler of beings, he is the protector of beings. He is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded. Brahmins seek to know him through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting. Only by knowing him does one become a sage (*muni*). Desiring this world alone, wandering mendicants go forth into homelessness.

Indeed, knowing this, those of old did not desire offspring, saying, "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this self is the world? They, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then lived the life of mendicants. For the desire for sons is the same as the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is the same as the desire for worlds; these two are indeed both just desires.

This very Self is "not this, not this. It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; indestructible, for it is not destroyed; unattached, for it is not attached; unfettered, it does not tremble, nor is it harmed. Indeed, these two do not cross over this [Self]: "I have done evil" and "I have done good. For he crosses over both; neither what has been done nor what has not been done afflicts him. (4.4.22)
This very thing has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse:
"This is the eternal greatness of a Brāhmaṇa; he does not increase by action, nor does he become less. Having known the path of that very [Self], one is not tainted by evil action."

Therefore, one who knows this, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and composed, sees the Self in the very Self; he sees the All as the Self. Evil does not overcome him; he overcomes all evil. Evil does not burn him; he burns up all evil. Free from evil, free from stain, and free from doubt, he becomes a Brahmin. "This is the world of Brahman, O Emperor," said Yājñavalkya, "you have reached it. "I give the Videhas to you, sir, and myself along with them," he replied. 4.4.23.

"Verily, this great unborn Self is the eater of food and the giver of wealth; he who knows this finds wealth. Verily, this great unborn Self is ageless, deathless, immortal, fearless Brahman. Brahman is indeed fearless. He who knows this becomes, verily, the fearless Brahman. (4.4.24–25)
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa.

Now, Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī. Of them, Maitreyī was a seeker of Brahman, while Kātyāyanī possessed only the common wisdom of women. Then Yājñavalkya prepared to enter upon another stage of life.
"Maitreyī," Yājñavalkya said, "I am indeed about to depart from this state. Come, let me make a final settlement for you with Kātyāyanī. (4.5.2)

Maitreyī said: "If, O Venerable Sir, this entire earth filled with wealth were mine, would I indeed become immortal by means of it, or not? "No," said Yājñavalkya, "your life would be just like the life of those who possess worldly means; there is no hope for immortality through wealth. (4.5.3)
Maitreyī said: "What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal? Tell me only that which you know, O Venerable One. (4.5.4)

Yājñavalkya said: "Truly, my dear lady, being already dear to us, you have increased what is dear. Well then, my dear, I shall explain this to you; but as I am explaining, you must meditate upon it. 4.5.5.

He said: "Truly, it is not out of love for the husband that the husband is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the husband is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the wife that the wife is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the wife is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the sons that the sons are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the sons are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for wealth that wealth is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that wealth is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for cattle that cattle are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that cattle are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the Brahminhood that the Brahminhood is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the Brahminhood is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the Kshatriyahood that the Kshatriyahood is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the Kshatriyahood is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the worlds that the worlds are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the worlds are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the gods that the gods are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the gods are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the Vedas that the Vedas are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the Vedas are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for beings that beings are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that beings are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for everything that everything is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that everything is dear."

"Verily, Maitreyī, the Self (ātman) must be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. Verily, when the Self has been seen, heard, reflected upon, and known, all this is known. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6)

Brahman abandons him who knows Brahman as other than the Self; the Kṣatra abandons him who knows the Kṣatra as other than the Self; the worlds abandon him who knows the worlds as other than the Self; the gods abandon him who knows the gods as other than the Self; the Vedas abandon him who knows the Vedas as other than the Self; beings abandon him who knows beings as other than the Self; everything abandons him who knows everything as other than the Self. This is Brahman, this is the Kṣatra, these are the worlds, these are the gods, these are the Vedas, these are beings, this is everything—that which is this Self.

"Just as, when a drum is being beaten, one cannot grasp its external sounds; yet by grasping the drum, or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped. (4.5.8) Just as, when a conch is being blown, one cannot grasp its external sounds; yet by grasping the conch, or the blowing of the conch, the sound is grasped. (4.5.9) Just as, when a lute is being played, one cannot grasp its external sounds; yet by grasping the lute, or the playing of the lute, the sound is grasped. (4.5.10) Just as, from a fire kindled with damp fuel, various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, my dear, these—the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharvāngirasa, history, ancient lore, sciences, Upanishads, verses, aphorisms, explanations, commentaries, what is sacrificed, what is offered, what is given, what is eaten, what is drunk, this world and the next world, and all beings—these are the breath of this Great Being. All these are indeed His breaths. (4.5.11) "Just as the ocean is the one goal of all waters, even so the skin is the one goal of all touches; the two nostrils are the one goal of all smells; the tongue is the one goal of all tastes; the eye is the one goal of all forms; the ear is the one goal of all sounds; the mind is the one goal of all thoughts; the heart is the one goal of all knowledges; the two hands are the one goal of all actions; the organ of generation is the one goal of all pleasures; the anus is the one goal of all excretions; the two feet are the one goal of all movements; speech is the one goal of all Vedas. (4.5.12) "Just as a mass of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a solid mass of taste, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a solid mass of consciousness. Arising from these elements, it vanishes back into them. After death there is no consciousness," thus I say, my dear. So spoke Yājñavalkya. (4.5.13)"

Maitreyī said: "In this very matter, my lord, you have plunged me into utter confusion; indeed, I do not understand this. He said: "Truly, I am not speaking of confusion, for this Self, my dear, is indestructible and its nature is such that it does not perish.

For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another; there one smells another; there one tastes another; there one speaks to another; there one hears another; there one thinks of another; there one touches another; there one perceives another. But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see? Then by what and whom should one smell? Then by what and whom should one taste? Then by what and to whom should one speak? Then by what and whom should one hear? Then by what and of whom should one think? Then by what and whom should one touch? Then by what and whom should one perceive? By what, my dear Maitreyī, should one perceive that by which one perceives all this? This very Self is "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; indestructible, for it is not destroyed; unattached, for it is not attached; unfettered—it neither trembles nor suffers injury. "By what, my dear Maitreyī, should one perceive the perceiver? This is the instruction I have given you. "This much indeed, my dear, is immortality. Having said this, Yājñavalkya departed. 4.5.15.
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa.

Now, the lineage (*vaṃśa*): Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana; Gaupavana from Pautimāṣya; Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana; Gaupavana from Kauśika; Kauśika from Kauṇḍinya; Kauṇḍinya from Śāṇḍilya; Śāṇḍilya from both Kauśika and Gautama; [and] Gautama from Agniveśya; Agniveśya from Gārgya; Gārgya from Gārgya; Gārgya from Gautama; Gautama from Saitava; Saitava from Pārāśaryāyaṇa; Pārāśaryāyaṇa from Gārgyāyaṇa; Gārgyāyaṇa from Uddālakāyana; Uddālakāyana from Jābālāyana; Jābālāyana from Mādhyandināyana; Mādhyandināyana from Saukarāyaṇa; Saukarāyaṇa from Kāṣāyaṇa; Kāṣāyaṇa from Sāyakāyana; Sāyakāyana from Kauśikāyani; Kauśikāyani from Ghṛtakauśika; Ghṛtakauśika from Pārāśaryāyaṇa; Pārāśaryāyaṇa from Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Jātukarṇya; Jātukarṇya from both Āsurāyaṇa and Yaska; Āsurāyaṇa from Traivaṇi; Traivaṇi from Aupajandhani; Aupajandhani from Āsuri; Āsuri from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from Ātreya; Ātreya from Māṇṭi; Māṇṭi from Gautama; Gautama from Gautama; Gautama from Vātsya; Vātsya from Śāṇḍilya; Śāṇḍilya from Kaiśorya Kāpya; Kaiśorya Kāpya from Kumārahārita; Kumārahārita from Gālava; Gālava from Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya; Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya from Vatsanapāt Bābhrava; Vatsanapāt Bābhrava from Pathas Saubhara; Panthas Saubhara from Ayāsya Āṅgirasa; Ayāsya Āṅgirasa from Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra; Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra from Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra; Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra from the two Aśvins; the two Aśvins from Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa from Atharvan Daiva; Atharvan Daiva from Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana; Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana from Pradhvaṃsana; Pradhvaṃsana from Ekarṣi; Ekarṣi from Vipracitti; Vipracitti from Vyaṣṭi; Vyaṣṭi from Sanāru; Sanāru from Sanātana; Sanātana from Sanaga; Sanaga from Parameṣṭhin; Parameṣṭhin from Brahmā; Brahmā is self-existent (*svayambhu*). Homage to Brahmā!
Thus ends the sixth Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
That is full, this is full; from the full, the full is drawn forth.
When the full is taken from the full, the full alone remains.
"Oṃ, Khaṃ is Brahman; Khaṃ is the ancient; Khaṃ is the wind. Thus indeed said Kauravyāyaṇīputra. "The Brahmins know this as the Veda; by means of this Veda, that which is to be known is known. 5.1.1.
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa.

There were three groups of Prajāpati’s offspring who lived the life of a religious student with their father Prajāpati: the gods, humans, and asuras. Having completed their studentship, the gods said, "May your honor speak to us. To them he spoke this syllable: "Da. "Do you understand? he asked. "We understand," they replied. "You have told us 'Be self-controlled' (dāmyata)," [he said]. "Yes," he said, "you have understood. (5.2.1)

Then the men said to him, "May your honor speak to us. He spoke this very syllable to them: "Da. [They asked: "Did you understand? They replied, "We understood. [He said: "Did you say 'da-tta' (give) to us? He said, "Om; you have understood. 5.2.2.

Then the Asuras said to him, "May your honor speak to us. He spoke this very syllable to them: "Da. "Have you understood? [he asked]. "We have understood," they replied. "Do you say 'Be compassionate' (dayadhvam) to us? "Yes," he said, "I have understood. Now, it is this very same divine voice that the thunder repeats: "Da-da-da"—that is, "Be self-controlled (damyata), give (datta), be compassionate (dayadhvam). Therefore, one should learn these three: self-control, giving, and compassion. 5.2.3.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa.

This heart is Prajāpati; this is Brahman; this is all. This "hṛdayam" consists of three syllables: *hṛ* is one syllable; to him who knows this, both his own people and others bring offerings. *da* is one syllable; to him who knows this, both his own people and others give gifts. *yam* is one syllable; he who knows this goes to the heavenly world. 5.3.1.
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa.

That indeed was this very thing; it was truth alone. He who knows this great, first-born being as the Brahman that is truth conquers these worlds; he has indeed already conquered them—he who thus knows this great, first-born being as the Brahman that is truth. For Brahman is indeed truth. 5.4.1.
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa.

In the beginning, this world was indeed only water. Those waters produced the Real (satya). The Real produced Brahman. Brahman produced Prajāpati. Prajāpati produced the gods. Those gods worship only the Real. This "Real" consists of three syllables: *sa* is one syllable, *ti* is one syllable, and *yam* is one syllable. The first and last syllables are the Real; the middle one is the Unreal. This Unreal is enclosed on both sides by the Real and thus becomes, as it were, of the nature of the Real. The Unreal does not harm one who knows this. 5.5.1.

That which is the Truth is yonder sun. The person who is in this orb and the person who is here in the right eye—these two are established in one another: by means of its rays, that [sun] is established in this [eye], and by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), this [eye] is established in that [sun]. When he is about to depart, he sees this orb as pure; these rays do not return to him. 5.5.2.

That person who is here in this orb—of him, *bhūr* is the head; there is one head, and this syllable is one. *Bhuvaḥ* is the two arms; there are two arms, and these two syllables are two. *Svar* is the foundation; there are two foundations, and these two syllables are two. His secret name (*upaniṣad*) is *ahaḥ*. He who knows thus destroys evil and leaves it behind. 5.5.3.

This person who is in the right eye—of him, *bhūḥ* is the head; there is one head, and this is one syllable. *Bhuvaḥ* is the two arms; there are two arms, and these are two syllables. *Svar* is the foundation; there are two foundations, and these are two syllables. His secret name (*upaniṣad*) is *aham* ("I"). He who knows this slays evil and leaves it behind. 5.5.4.
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa.

This person consists of mind, is of the nature of light, and is true; he is within this heart, like a grain of rice or a grain of barley. He is the ruler of all, the lord of all, who governs all this, whatever exists. 5.6.1.
Thus ends the sixth Brāhmaṇa.

"Lightning is Brahman," they say. It is called lightning because it flashes (*vidāna*). He who knows that "lightning is Brahman" is illuminated by it from evil; for lightning is indeed Brahman. 5.7.1.
Thus ends the seventh Brāhmaṇa.

One should worship speech as a cow. It has four udders: the utterance *svāhā*, the utterance *vaṣaṭ*, the utterance *hanta*, and the utterance *svadhā*. Two of its udders the gods subsist upon: the *svāhā* and the *vaṣaṭ*. Humans subsist upon the *hanta*, and the ancestors upon the *svadhā*. Its bull is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and its calf is the mind (*manas*). 5.8.1.
Thus ends the eighth Brāhmaṇa.

This is Agni Vaiśvānara, who is within the person, by whom this food is digested—this which is eaten. Its sound becomes audible when one covers the ears and hears it. When he is about to depart [from the body], he no longer hears that sound. 5.9.1.
Thus ends the ninth Brāhmaṇa.

When a person departs from this world, he goes to the wind. There, the wind parts for him as the hole of a chariot wheel. By that opening he ascends upward. He reaches the sun. There, the sun parts for him as the hole of a *lambara* drum. By that opening he ascends upward. He reaches the moon. There, the moon parts for him as the hole of a kettle-drum. By that opening he ascends upward. He reaches the world that is free from sorrow and free from cold. There he dwells for eternal years. 5.10.1.
Thus ends the tenth Brāhmaṇa.

This indeed is the highest austerity: when one who is emaciated performs penance. He who knows this wins the highest world. This indeed is the highest austerity: when they carry the deceased to the forest. He who knows this wins the highest world. This indeed is the highest austerity: when they place the deceased upon the fire. He who knows this wins the highest world. 5.11.1.
Thus ends the eleventh Brāhmaṇa.

"Food is Brahman," so some say. That is not so; for food putrefies without life-breath (*prāṇa*). "Life-breath is Brahman," so some say. That is not so; for life-breath withers without food. But these two deities, having become one, attain the supreme state. Regarding this, Prātṛda once said to his father: "What good could I do for one who knows this? Or what evil could I do to him? He [the father] replied, "Do not touch me with your hand, Prātṛda! Who can attain the supreme state by becoming one with these two? To him he then spoke this: "Vi. Food is indeed "vi," for all these beings are pervaded (*viṣṭa*) by food. "Ram. Life-breath is indeed "ram," for all these beings delight (*ramante*) in life-breath. Indeed, all beings enter into him and all beings delight in him who knows this. 5.12.1.1.12.1–20.10 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.12.1)
Thus ends the twelfth Brāhmaṇa.

The *uktha*. The *uktha* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for the vital breath raises up all this. A hero who knows the *uktha* stands firm because of it. He who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as the *uktha*. 5.13.1.

The Yajus. The vital breath (prāṇa) indeed is the Yajus; for in the vital breath all these beings are joined together. All beings are joined to him for preeminence who knows this, and he wins union with and residence in the same world as the Yajus. 5.13.2.

Sāman. Breath indeed is Sāman, for in breath all these beings are united (*samyañci*). All beings become united for his preeminence; he who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as Sāman. 5.13.3.

The ruling power (*kṣatra*). The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the ruling power; for the vital breath is indeed the ruling power. The vital breath protects him from being harmed; he attains the state of a ruler and reaches the state of a non-ruler. He who knows this wins union with the ruling power and residence in the same world as it. 5.13.4.
Thus ends the thirteenth Brāhmaṇa.

"Earth, intermediate space, and heaven"—these are eight syllables. Now, one foot of the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables; this indeed is that [foot] of hers. As far as these three worlds extend, so far indeed does he conquer who knows this foot of hers in this way.

The *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman* chants—these are eight syllables. Now, one foot of the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables; this very thing constitutes that [foot] of hers. As great as this threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) is, so much does he conquer who knows this foot of hers in this way. (5.14.2)

"Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna"—these are eight syllables. Indeed, one foot of the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables; this very [foot] of hers is that. As far as there is anything living here, so much does he conquer who knows this foot of hers thus. Now, this is her fourth, visible foot, which shines beyond the dust—that which is yonder burning. For what is fourth is the "fourth" (turīya). "The visible foot": for it is, as it were, visible. "Beyond the dust": for it burns entirely above and beyond the dust. In this very way, he who knows this foot of hers thus shines with splendor and fame. 5.14.3.

This very Gāyatrī is established upon that fourth, visible foot, beyond the dust of the earth. That, indeed, is established upon Truth. Sight is Truth; for sight, indeed, is Truth. Therefore, if two people should come disputing, one saying "I saw it" and the other "I heard it," we would believe the one who says "I saw it. That Truth, indeed, is established upon Strength. Breath is Strength; thus it is established upon Breath. Therefore they say, "Strength is more powerful than Truth. Thus this Gāyatrī is established within the self (adhyātma). She protected the *gayas*. The *gayas* are the vital breaths (*prāṇas*); she protected the vital breaths. Because she protected the *gayas*, she is named Gāyatrī. This Sāvitrī which one recites is indeed this very same one. Whomever one recites it for, she protects his vital breaths. 5.14.4.

Some recite this Sāvitrī as an Anuṣṭubh verse, saying, "The Anuṣṭubh is speech; thus we recite speech. One should not do so. One should recite the Sāvitrī as a Gāyatrī verse alone. For even if one who knows this accepts much in the way of gifts, it does not equal even a single foot of the Gāyatrī.

If one were to receive these three worlds full, he would obtain only this first foot of her. And if one were to receive as much as this triple knowledge (the Vedas) exists, he would obtain this second foot of her. And if one were to receive as many living beings as exist here, he would obtain this third foot of her. But her fourth, visible foot, which is beyond the dust and shines yonder—that which burns—is not to be obtained by anyone at all. How, then, could one receive even that much? 5.14.6.

The worship of it: "Gāyatrī, you are one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed; you are footless, for you do not walk. Homage to your fourth, visible foot, which is beyond the dust of the world! May so-and-so reach that [state]," or, "May such-and-such a desire not be fulfilled for him whom I hate. Indeed, that desire is never fulfilled for the one whom he thus worships, or [he says], "I have reached that [state]. (5.14.7)

Janaka of Videha said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi: "How is it that you, who claim to know the Gāyatrī, now carry an elephant? How is it that you have become an elephant? He replied: "O King, I did not know its mouth. "Fire indeed is its mouth," he said. "For even if they throw much fuel into the fire, it consumes it all. In the same way, even if one who knows this performs much evil, it consumes it all; he becomes pure, cleansed, ageless, and immortal. (5.14.8)
Thus ends the fourteenth Brāhmaṇa.
The face of truth is covered by a golden vessel;
O Pūṣan, uncover it for me, who am devoted to the law of truth, so that I may see.
O Pūṣan, sole seer, Yama, Sūrya, son of Prajāpati, spread out your rays and gather back your splendor! That form of yours which is most auspicious—that I behold. That person who is yonder, that am I.
Vāyu [is] the breath, the immortal; and this body ends in ashes. Om! O Kratu, remember; remember what was done. O Kratu, remember; remember what was done.
O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knowest all ways;
keep far from us the sin that leads astray, and we shall offer unto thee the most abundant speech of homage. 5.15.1.
Thus ends the fifteenth Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.

Verily, he who knows the oldest and the best becomes the oldest and the best among his own people. Breath indeed is the oldest and the best. He who knows this becomes the oldest and the best among his own people, and even among those whom he wishes to excel. 6.1.1.

He who knows the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhā*) becomes the most excellent among his own people. Speech indeed is the most excellent. He who knows this becomes the most excellent among his own people, and also among those whom he desires to excel. 6.1.2.

He who knows the foundation indeed finds a firm footing; he stands firm on level ground and stands firm on rough terrain. The eye, indeed, is the foundation. For by means of the eye one stands firm on both level ground and rough terrain. He who knows thus stands firm on level ground and stands firm on rough terrain. 6.1.3.

Verily, he who knows attainment—for him whatever desire he desires is attained. The ear, indeed, is attainment; for in the ear all these Vedas are fully contained. For him who knows this, whatever desire he desires is attained. 6.1.4.

He who knows the abode indeed becomes the abode of his own people and the abode of other men. The mind, indeed, is the abode. He who knows thus becomes the abode of his own people and the abode of other men. 6.1.5
He who knows procreation indeed procreates with offspring and cattle. Semen is procreation. He who knows thus procreates with offspring and cattle. (6.1.6)

These vital breaths (*prāṇas*), disputing among themselves as to who was the best, went to Brahmā. They said to him, "Which of us is the most excellent? He replied, "He among you, upon whose departure this body is considered the worst off—he is the most excellent of you. (6.1.7)

Speech departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the dumb live without speech—breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen—even so did we live. Then Speech entered back in. 6.1.8.

The eye departed. Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "We lived just as blind people do—seeing with the eye, breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen. Then the eye entered back in. 6.1.9.

The ear departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the deaf live—without hearing with the ear, yet breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen—even so did we live. Then the ear entered back in. 6.1.10.

The mind departed. Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the ignorant and simple-minded live—breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and procreating with semen—even so did we live. Then the mind entered back in. 6.1.11.

The semen departed. Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as eunuchs live without procreating—breathing with breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and knowing with the mind—so have we lived. Then the semen entered back in. 6.1.12.

Then, as the vital breath was about to depart, it tore out these other breaths just as a great Sindhava horse might tear up its tethering pegs. They said, "O Venerable One, do not depart! We shall certainly not be able to live without you. He said, "Then offer me tribute. They said, "So be it. 6.1.13.

Speech said: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent; insofar as I am the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), you are that foundation"—thus spoke the eye. "Insofar as I am prosperity (*saṃpat*), you are that prosperity"—thus spoke the ear. "Insofar as I am the abode (*āyatana*), you are that abode"—thus spoke the mind. "Insofar as I am procreation (*prajāti*), you are that procreation"—thus spoke semen. [The Breath asked: "What, then, is my food? What is my clothing? "Whatever there is here, even unto dogs, worms, insects, and moths—that is your food; water is your clothing. Indeed, for one who knows this food of breath, no food is ever eaten that is not food, nor is anything received that is not food. Therefore, learned Vedic scholars, when about to eat, sip water, and after eating, they sip water; thus they consider themselves to have made this very food free from nakedness. 61.14.
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa.

Śvetaketu Āruṇeya went to the assembly of the Pañcālas. He approached Pravāhaṇa Jaibali while he was being waited upon. Looking up at him, [Jaibali] addressed him, saying, "Young man! He replied, "Sir! [Jaibali asked], "Have you been instructed by your father? "Yes," he said. (6.2.1)

"Do you know how these creatures, when they depart, diverge? "No," he said. "Do you know how they return again to this world? "No indeed," he said. "Do you know why that world is not filled up, even though many go there again and again? "No indeed," he said. "Do you know at which oblation, when offered, the waters, having become human speech, arise and speak? "No indeed," he said. "Do you know the point of entry for the path of the gods or the path of the fathers—that which, having performed, people enter upon the path of the gods or the path of the fathers? For we have heard the word of the seer:"
"I have heard of two paths for the fathers—those of the gods and those of mortals. Along these two, all this moving world comes together, that which lies between the father and the mother.
"I do not know even one of them," he said. (6.2.2)

Then he invited him to stay for the night. But disregarding the invitation to stay, the youth ran away. He went to his father and said to him, "Sir, you have indeed told us that we were instructed by you previously. [The father asked,] "How so, Sumedha? [He replied,] "A kinsman of the royal class asked me five questions; of those, I did not know even one. [The father asked,] "Which ones were they? And he recited the beginnings of them. 6.2.3.

He said, "O son, you should know us thus: whatever I know, all that I have told you. But come, let us go there and dwell as students of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya). "May you yourself go," [the other replied]. So Gautama went to where Pravāhaṇa Jaibali was. Having offered him a seat, he had water brought for him. Then he offered him the guest-offering (arghya). He said to him, "We grant a boon to the venerable Gautama. (6.2.4)
He said, "This boon has been promised to me; however, tell me that word which you spoke in the presence of the boy."
He said, "Gautama, those [boons] are indeed among the divine; speak for those of men."

He said, "It is indeed known that I have received gold, cattle, horses, female slaves, attendants, and clothing. May you not, sir, be one who diminishes me from what is so much, endless, and boundless. "Gautama, do you desire [this] by way of the sacred ford? "I am approaching you as a pupil," he replied. Formerly, they used to approach [a teacher] merely with words; thus he dwelt there, announcing his arrival as a student.

He said: "In this way, O Gautama, do not offend us, nor your ancestors, since this knowledge has never before dwelt with any Brāhmaṇa. Nevertheless, I shall tell it to you; for who indeed would refuse one who speaks thus? (6.2.8)

That world, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama. Of that, the sun is the fuel, the rays are the smoke, the day is the flame, the quarters are the embers, and the intermediate quarters are the sparks. Into this very fire, the gods offer faith. From that oblation, King Soma comes into being. 6.2.9.

"Parjanya, O Gautama, is indeed Agni. Of him, the year is the fuel, the clouds are the smoke, lightning is the flame, thunderbolts are the embers, and peals of thunder are the sparks. Into this very fire, the gods offer King Soma. From that offering, rain comes into being. (6.2.10)

This world, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama. Of this fire, the earth is the fuel, fire is the smoke, night is the flame, the moon is the embers, and the stars are the sparks. Into this very fire, the gods offer rain. From that oblation, food comes into being. 6.2.11.

"Man, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama. His opened mouth is the fuel; his breath is the smoke; his speech is the flame; his eye is the embers; his ear is the sparks. Into this very fire, the gods offer food. From that oblation, semen comes into being. (6.2.12)

Woman, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama. Her lap is the kindling wood; her body hair is the smoke; her vulva is the flame; what she does within is the embers; her pleasures are the sparks. Into this very fire the gods offer semen. From that oblation a person comes into being. He lives as long as he lives. Then, when he dies... 6.2.13

Then they carry him to the fire. Of that [fire], the fire itself becomes the fire; the fuel becomes the fuel; the smoke becomes the smoke; the flame becomes the flame; the embers become the embers; the sparks become the sparks. Into this very fire, the gods offer the person. From that oblation, the person comes into being with a radiant complexion. 6.2.14.

Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, venerate truth with faith—they pass into the light. From the light they go to the day; from the day to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight to the six months during which the sun moves northward; from those months to the world of the gods; from the world of the gods to the sun; and from the sun to the lightning. A person consisting of mind comes to those [beings] in the lightning and leads them to the worlds of Brahman. In those worlds of Brahman, they dwell for the highest of high distances. For them there is no return. 6.2.15.

Now, those who win worlds through sacrifice, through charity, and through austerity, they attain the smoke; from smoke, the night; from the night, the waning fortnight; from the waning fortnight, those six months during which the sun moves southward; from those months, the world of the fathers; from the world of the fathers, the moon. Having reached the moon, they become food. There, the gods consume them, just as they consume King Soma with the words, "Swell up! Wane away! When that [merit] of theirs is exhausted, they emerge into this very space; from space, into the air; from the air, into rain; from rain, onto the earth. Having reached the earth, they become food. They are offered again into the fire of man, and from there they are born in the fire of woman. Thus do they revolve, returning to the worlds. But those who know not these two paths become worms, moths, and whatever is biting. 6.2.16.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa.

He who should desire, "May I attain greatness," should, during the northern course of the sun, on an auspicious day of the waxing moon, having observed the *upasad* vow for twelve days, collect all kinds of herbs and fruits in a vessel or cup made of *udumbara* wood; then, having swept around, smeared [the ground], kindled the fire, and strewn grass around it, he should prepare clarified butter according to the prescribed rite, mix a mash under an asterism associated with a male deity, and offer it as a sacrifice:
"O Jātavedas, as many gods as dwell within you, who strike down the desires of a man by their transverse ways..."

To them I offer my portion; may they, being satisfied, satisfy me with all my desires—*svāhā*. O thou who, lying across, sayest "I am the supporter," thee, the propitiator, I worship with a stream of clarified butter—*svāhā*. (6.3.1)
Having offered in the fire with the words, "To the eldest, svāhā! To the best, svāhā! he pours the remnants into the mash.
With the words, "To the out-breath, svāhā!
To the most excellent, svāhā! having offered in the fire, he pours the remnants into the mash. [With the words,] "To speech, svāhā!"

Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To stability, svāhā," he pours the remnants into the stirred drink. Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To sight, svāhā;

to success, svāhā," he pours the remnants into the stirred drink. Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To hearing, svāhā; to the abode, svāhā," he pours the remnants into the stirred drink. [He offers] "To the mind, svāhā."

Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To procreation, svāhā!", he pours the residue into the mash. Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To semen, svāhā!", he pours the residue into the mash. 6.3.2.

Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to Agni," he pours the residue into the mash. Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to Soma," he pours the residue into the mash. Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Bhūḥ Svāhā," he pours the residue into the mash. Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā," he pours the residue into the mash.
